doi:10.1016/j.ygyno.2026.09.018.abstract: To determine whether plasma and serum extracellular vesicles (EV) are interchangeable for immunoaffinity-enriched proteomic profiling in high-grade serous ovarian cancer (HGSOC), and whether an EV protein signature improves diagnostic performance beyond CA-125 for detecting ovarian cancer. We performed immunoaffinity-enriched proteomic profiling of EV subpopulations from 243 paired EDTA plasma and serum samples in a nested case-control cohort from the UK Ovarian Cancer Population Study (controls, benign, borderline, and HGSOC). Analyses assessed proteomic depth, plasma-serum concordance, and diagnostic performance using machine learning. Plasma-derived EV subpopulations showed greater proteomic depth than serum, with 6439 versus 5451 protein groups identified and 2838 versus 840 proteins detected at 50% prevalence. Protein intensities were highly concordant between matrices (r = 0.86, p < 0.001), maintained across disease groups and cancer stages. For distinguishing HGSOC from non-cancers, an EV-augmented CA-125 model achieved an AUROC of 0.97 in plasma and 0.96 in serum, improving plasma sensitivity to 99% (95% CI 89-100) and specificity to 85% (95% CI 68-91) versus 96% (95% CI 82-100) sensitivity and 65% (95% CI 15-73) specificity for CA-125 alone, with similarly high discrimination in serum. Surface epitope-targeted EV subpopulation enrichment yields specific proteomic profiling of HGSOC with highly concordant biomarker signatures across plasma and serum, supporting their interchangeable use in clinical and biobank settings. The EV-augmented CA-125 model outperformed CA-125 alone, with recurrent EV proteins reflecting mucin-mediated immune evasion, and metabolic reprogramming, underscoring the translational potential of this approach for blood-based ovarian cancer detection.

doi:10.1016/j.ygyno.2026.10.004.abstract: Metformin is a potential anticancer agent; however, evidence of benefit in endometrial neoplasia is limited. We evaluated whether adding metformin improved the outcomes of progestin-based fertility-sparing treatment. In this multicenter, open-label, randomized, phase IIb trial using blinded central adjudication, women aged 18-42years with an institutional diagnosis of atypical endometrial hyperplasia (AEH) or presumed stage IA grade 1 endometrioid carcinoma were assigned (1:1:1) to medroxyprogesterone acetate (MPA) alone, MPA plus metformin 750mg/day, or MPA plus metformin 1500mg/day. Central pathological review reclassified baseline specimens according to the 2020 World Health Organization criteria and adjudicated remission and recurrence. The primary endpoint was the 3-year recurrence-free survival (RFS) rate from treatment initiation. Secondary endpoints included remission, pregnancy outcomes, and safety. Analysis included 154 patients. Median body mass index was 24.3 (range, 15.6-57.1) kg/m2. The Kaplan-Meier estimates of the 3-year RFS rate were 44.7% with MPA alone and 44.5% with the pooled metformin groups. The prespecified log-rank test showed no significant difference (P=0.825). Remission rates were 54.0%, 58.8%, and 50.9% in the MPA-alone, metformin 750mg, and metformin 1500mg groups, respectively. Among the 57 women who attempted to conceive, pregnancy occurred in 36.8%, 57.9%, and 42.1%, and live birth in 31.6%, 52.6%, and 31.6%, respectively. Metformin increased gastrointestinal adverse events and was associated with less MPA-associated weight gain; no new safety signals emerged. Adding metformin to MPA did not improve RFS or remission rates, suggesting limited benefit in fertility-sparing treatment of endometrial neoplasia.

doi:10.1016/j.ygyno.2026.10.005.abstract: As immunotherapy (IO) is increasingly utilized for treatment of endometrial cancer (EC) and cervical cancer (CC), optimal treatment strategies after IO remains poorly defined. We evaluated clinical outcomes, treatment patterns, toxicity, and survival among patients with recurrent EC and CC who received IO after prior IO. An Institutional Review Board approved, single-institution retrospective cohort study was conducted among patients with recurrent EC or CC treated with subsequent IO between January 1, 2017, and January 1, 2025. Patients were included if they received at least one dose of IO after prior IO. Clinical characteristics, immune-related adverse events, response, progression-free survival (PFS), and overall survival (OS) were abstracted from the electronic medical record. Of fifty eligible patients, 36 had EC and 14 had CC. Pembrolizumab was the most common first IO agent in both cohorts. Second IO regimens differed by disease site, with pembrolizumab plus lenvatinib most common in EC and pembrolizumab alone most common in CC. Following second IO exposure, objective response rate was 27.8% for EC and 14.3% for CC, while disease control rate was 55.6% and 64.3%, respectively. Median PFS with second IO exposure was 8.1 months in EC and 9.7 months in CC. Grade 3/4 immune-related adverse events occurred in 20.0% during second IO. IO retreatment demonstrated clinical activity in selected patients with recurrent EC and CC after prior IO, with disease control achieved in more than half of patients. Prospective studies are needed to define optimal patient selection and post-IO treatments.

doi:10.1016/j.ygyno.2026.10.006.abstract: The PERSONA-Ovary study evaluated germline pathogenic/likely-pathogenic variant prevalence, feasibility of unselected multigene testing integration in routine clinical care, and germline-somatic BRCA concordance in ovarian cancer patients. We conducted a prospective observational study of consecutive ovarian carcinoma patients treated at a tertiary-cancer care center, between July 2018 and September 2021. Germline multigene panel testing was performed using next-generation sequencing. Feasibility was assessed by informative rate and turnaround time. Germline-somatic concordance was assessed in patients with paired tumor BRCA results. Among 320 patients, pathogenic/likely-pathogenic variants were identified in 95 (29.7%, 95% CI 24.7-35.0); 81 (85.3%, 95% CI 76.5-91.7) carried mutations in ovarian cancer susceptibility genes, including 60 with BRCA alterations (63.2%, BRCA1 n=43, BRCA2 n=17). Germline testing was informative in all patients (100%). Median turnaround time was 221days (IQR 173-284), improving significantly across study periods (p<0.001). Tumor BRCA testing was available in 298 patients (93.1%), with germline-somatic concordance of 94.0% (κ=0.82, 95% CI 0.72-0.90). A germline-first strategy with reflex tumor testing achieved complete detection with fewer assays than parallel testing; a tumor-first strategy required the fewest assays (366 vs 596) but missed two germline BRCA carriers (detection rate of 96.3%). Unselected germline multigene panel testing was technically feasible and clinically informative in routine ovarian cancer care. Pathogenic/likely-pathogenic variants were identified in 29.7% of patients, supporting germline testing integration into contemporary ovarian cancer management. Although germline-first strategies maximize hereditary cancer detection, dedicated molecular workflows remain necessary to ensure clinically actionable turnaround times.

doi:10.1016/j.ygyno.2026.10.007.abstract: To evaluate the impact of adjuvant chemotherapy on oncologic outcomes in patients with surgically staged 2009 FIGO stage I uterine serous carcinoma (USC) and to assess the prognostic significance of peritoneal cytology. We retrospectively reviewed patients who underwent surgery at our institution for newly diagnosed, 2009 FIGO stage I USC. Outcomes were stratified by depth of myometrial invasion. We identified 327 patients: 185 (56.6%) with non-myoinvasive disease, 113 (34.6%) with <50% myometrial invasion, and 29 (8.9%) with ≥50% myometrial invasion. Among patients with any myoinvasion, the 5-year PFS was 54.4% (95% CI: 35%-70.2%) for no chemotherapy versus 62.6% (95% CI: 52.2%-71.3%) for chemotherapy (P = 0.10), and the 5-year OS was 52.3% (95% CI: 33.4%-68.2%) versus 79.9% (95% CI: 70.4%-86.6%), respectively (P = 0.008). Use of chemotherapy was independently associated with improved PFS (adjusted HR, 0.50 [95% CI: 0.26-0.96]) and OS (adjusted HR, 0.42 [95% CI: 0.23-0.78]). For patients with non-myoinvasive disease and negative cytology, the 5-year PFS was 89.5% (95% CI: 83.4%-93.5%), and for those with positive cytology, it was 48.8% (95% CI: 22.8%-70.6%; HR, 0.19 [95% CI: 0.08-0.44]). In this patient cohort, postoperative adjuvant chemotherapy was associated with improved survival when myoinvasion was present but did not appear to confer a survival benefit in the absence of myoinvasion. Malignant peritoneal cytology was strongly prognostic in non-myoinvasive disease, and these patients had outcomes resembling those with myoinvasive tumors. These findings support incorporating cytology status into adjuvant decision-making for stage I USC.

doi:10.1016/j.ygyno.2026.10.009.abstract: The survival outcomes of advanced or recurrent endometrial cancer (EC) have not improved markedly despite the expanding therapeutic options. We performed molecular characterization of EC to identify therapeutic targets and prognostic biomarkers. Whole-exome sequencing (WES)-based somatic mutation profiling was performed in tumor samples obtained from 67 EC patients (41 early-stage and 26 advanced/recurrent cases). The frequencies of somatic mutations were compared between early and advanced/recurrent EC. Copy number variation analysis was also performed. Survival outcomes and recurrences according to mutational status were analyzed. TP53 and KRAS mutations tended to be more frequent in advanced/recurrent disease than early-stage EC. Deletions were also more common in advanced EC (42.3% vs. 17.1%). Among the advanced EC patients (n=26), 16 patients recurred. Recurrent cases had significantly higher TP53 mutation rates (56.3% versus 10%) and lower PTEN mutation rates (25% versus 80%) than non-recurrent cases. KRAS and CTNNB1 mutations also tended to be enriched. Although KRAS mutation alone only showed a trend of shorter OS (p=0.179) in advanced EC, KRAS-TP53 co-mutation exhibited the worst survival outcomes (p=0.011). KRAS-TP53 co-mutation was associated with chemoresistance: all the co-mutated cases were chemoresistant, whereas patients without either mutation were chemosensitive. Among copy-number low (CNL) and microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H) tumors (n=46), KRAS-TP53 co-mutation was strongly associated with adverse survival outcomes (p=0.003). KRAS-TP53 co-mutation represents a potential molecular biomarker of poor prognosis and chemoresistance in advanced EC. It may enable refinement of TCGA classification, especially for CNL and MSI-H subgroups, and support investigation of KRAS-targeted therapeutic strategies.

doi:10.1016/j.ygyno.2026.10.010.abstract: To examine temporal trends in immunotherapy (IO) adoption and identify factor-related disparities among older adults with advanced endometrial cancer (EC). We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the National Cancer Database (NCDB), including women aged ≥65 years diagnosed with stage III-IV EC between 2019 and 2023. Temporal trends of IO use were assessed, and multivariable logistic regression identified predictors of IO utilization. Among 38,931 patients with advanced EC, 21,272 (54.6%) were aged ≥65 years. IO utilization increased significantly over time across all age groups (P-trend <0.001). By 2023, 1851 older adults (40%) received IO, but utilization remained substantially lower among patients aged ≥85 years (55/255, 21.6%; P < 0.001). On multivariable analysis, patients aged ≥85 years were significantly less likely to receive IO compared with those aged 65-74 years (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 0.41; 95% CI, 0.32-0.52; P < 0.001). Non-Hispanic (NH)-Black (aOR 0.81; 95% CI, 0.73-0.90; P < 0.001) and Hispanic patients (aOR 0.84; 95% CI, 0.71-0.99; P = 0.034) were also less likely to receive IO compared with NH-White patients. After adjustment for socioeconomic factors, NH-Black was 12% less likely to receive IO (aOR 0.88; 95% CI, 0.77-0.99; P = 0.0034). Despite the proven clinical benefit of IO use for patients with advanced EC, substantial age-based disparities persist. A lower likelihood of IO receipt among NH-Black compared with NH-White patients was also observed even after adjustment for socioeconomic factors. These findings highlight the need for further investigation into clinical, socioeconomic, and structural barriers influencing treatment access in older and minoritized populations.

doi:10.1038/s41375-026-03157-0.abstract: Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) is driven by the constitutively active BCR::ABL1 kinase, which promotes uncontrolled cell proliferation. Although protein-tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) have revolutionized CML treatment, resistance remains a significant barrier to curative therapy, particularly due to BCR::ABL1 mutations and the persistence of leukemia stem cells (LSCs). New treatment strategies that directly inhibit BCR::ABL1 protein expression are needed to achieve more effective therapy. Using a high-content antibody microarray and bioinformatics analyses, we investigated differences in the proteome and phosphorylation landscape of Imatinib (IM)-resistant cells and identified highly activated members of the eukaryotic translation initiation complex (eIF4F), particularly eIF4G1, a core component of eIF4F. These eIF4F complex members are highly expressed and activated in CD34+ CML stem/progenitor cells and in IM-resistant cells. Genetic inhibition of eIF4G1 or pharmacological targeting with the small-molecule inhibitor SBI-756 diminished eIF4F complex assembly, reduced overall translation initiation, reduced BCR::ABL1 expression and key downstream targets, impaired the survival of nonresponder stem/progenitor cells, including BCR::ABL1-T315I mutant cells, and sensitized them to TKIs, with strong synergistic effects in vitro and in a PDX model. These findings underscore the potential of eIF4F complex inhibition as a new therapeutic strategy to overcome TKI resistance in CML and other BCR::ABL1+ malignancies.

doi:10.1038/s41375-026-03159-y.abstract: Abstract CD24 is highly expressed in aggressive B-cell malignancies and represents a novel immunologic vulnerability to overcome resistance to CD19 chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy. We developed a CD24 × CD3 bispecific antibody (CD24 BsAb) and CXCR3-armed CD24 CAR-T cells, both exhibiting potent antitumor activity in lymphoma and leukemia models. CD24 BsAb and CD24 CAR-T overcome CD19 CAR-T resistance driven by antigen loss and apoptosis defects in vitro and in vivo. Beyond direct cytotoxicity, CD24-targeted T cells reprogram macrophages toward an M1-like phenotype and enhance phagocytic clearance. We further engineered a dual-specific, dual-functional CD19 CAR-T that secretes a CD24 bispecific T-cell engager (CD24 BiTE), enabling simultaneous targeting of CD19 and CD24 to address tumor heterogeneity and achieve superior efficacy. Collectively, our study demonstrates that CD24-directed adoptive T-cell therapies are warranted for B-cell malignancies through robust induction of both innate and adaptive immune responses.

doi:10.1038/s41375-026-03160-5.abstract: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) cells are highly dependent on mitochondrial activity for survival, with this metabolic reliance driven in part by BCL-2, which is therapeutically targeted by venetoclax-based therapies. The regulation of mitochondrial dynamics in leukemic cells is therefore essential for maintaining mitochondrial homeostasis. However, the mechanisms that enable selective degradation of damaged mitochondria (mitophagy) are still poorly understood in AML. In this study, we sought to elucidate the role of PTEN-induced putative kinase 1 (PINK1), a key sensor of mitochondrial stress, in regulating mitophagy in leukemic cells. Our results identified PINK1 as a central modulator of mitophagy. Genetic depletion of PINK1 reduced both basal and stress-induced mitophagy, leading to mitochondria accumulation and functional impairment. Additionally, we discovered that PINK1 stabilization during mitochondrial stress is regulated by Prohibitin 2 (PHB2), and that depletion or inhibition of PHB2 mirrored the biological effects of PINK1 loss. Notably, both genetic depletion of PINK1 or PHB2, as well as pharmacological inhibition of PHB2, significantly increased AML cell sensitivity to venetoclax both in vitro and in vivo. Together, these findings highlight the potential of targeting the PHB2/PINK1 signalling pathway to improve the efficacy of venetoclax-based therapies in AML by disrupting the mitophagy process.

doi:10.1038/s41375-026-03169-w.abstract: Aberrant expression of neoantigenic receptor ROR1 has been identified in diverse lymphomas, including mantle cell lymphoma (MCL) and in a broad spectrum of nonlymphoid malignancies. While ROR1 has emerged as an attractive therapeutic target, its oncogenic role and the underlying mechanisms remain rather poorly characterized. Focusing on MCL, we found that ROR1 expression is heterogeneous and it can be induced under environmental stress. Inhibition of ROR1 expression resulted in cell-cycle suppression and apoptotic cell death. The ROR1 loss affected expression of numerous genes and altered phosphorylation of many proteins, including those involved in cell-cycle progression. ROR1 also promotes the synthesis of pyrimidines and purines, including induction of phosphorylation of enzymes involved in pyrimidine synthesis. Finally, we found that ROR1 induced phosphorylation of DEK and that its depletion abrogates ROR1 expression. These results provide insights into the multi-faceted oncogenic role of ROR1, further justifying targeting ROR1 in MCL and other malignancies.

doi:10.1038/s41375-026-03177-w.abstract: We interrogated data from 217 subjects with primary myelofibrosis (PMF) diagnosed before 2001 to identify covariates at diagnosis associated with long-term survival. Forty-one survived more than 25 years. Long-term survivors were more often female, younger than 50 years and less likely to have anemia, splenomegaly, increased blood CD34-positive cells, a JAK2V617F variant, and more likely to have grade-0 bone marrow fibrosis and increased platelets. In multivariable logistic regression analyses, age 450 × 10⁹/L, and grade-0 bone marrow fibrosis independently predicted long-term survival. These co-variate associations were confirmed in Cox regression with landmark analyses. Long-term survivors had a lower cumulative incidence of anemia and thrombocytopenia during follow-up. Identifying long-term survivors at diagnosis provides clinically meaningful prognostic information in PMF and may influence therapy decisions.

doi:10.1038/s41388-024-02996-4.abstract: Abstract Colorectal cancer (CRC) has a high degree of heterogeneity and identifying the genetic information of individual tumor cells could help enhance our understanding of tumor biology and uncover potential therapeutic targets for CRC. In this study, we identified LPCAT2+ tumor cell populations with less malignancy than LPCAT2- tumor cells in human and mouse CRC tissues using scRNA-seq. Combining in vitro and in vivo experiments, we found that LPCAT2 could inhibit the proliferation of CRC cells by inducing ferroptosis. Mechanistically, LPCAT2 arrested PRMT1 in cytoplasm of CRC cells via regulating acetylation of PRMT1 at the K145 site. In turn, PRMT1 enhanced SLC7A11 promoter activity. Thus, LPCAT2 attenuated the positive regulatory effect of PRMT1 on SLC7A11 promoter. Notably, SLC7A11 acts as a ferroptosis regulator. Furthermore, in LPCAT2 knockout mice (LPCAT2−/−) colon cancer model, we found that LPCAT2−/− mice exhibited more severe lesions, while PRMT1 or SLC7A11 inhibitors delayed the progression. Altogether, we elucidated that LPCAT2 suppresses SLC7A11 expression by inhibiting PRMT1 nuclear translocation, thereby inducing ferroptosis in CRC cells. Moreover, inhibitors of the PRMT1/SLC7A11 axis could delay tumor progression in CRC with low LPCAT2 expression, making it a potentially effective treatment for CRC.

doi:10.1038/s41388-026-04008-z.abstract: T cell immunoreceptor with Ig and ITIM domains (TIGIT) is a key inhibitory receptor on cytotoxic lymphocytes, yet the mechanisms governing its context-dependent upregulation in tumors remain poorly defined. Here, we identify tumor necrosis factor-α (TNFα) signaling as an upstream driver of TIGIT expression. Integrated analyses of patient transcriptomic datasets revealed a consistent positive association between TNFα pathway activity and TIGIT expression across multiple cancer types, with strong concordance in melanoma and prognostic relevance in kidney renal clear cell carcinoma. Mechanistically, TNFα directly induced TIGIT expression in natural killer cells via TNFR2 signaling, increasing chromatin accessibility at distal TIGIT enhancers and promoting NF-κB and AP-1 recruitment together with BRD4 and P300. Functionally, combined anti-TNFα and anti-TIGIT treatment suppressed tumor growth and prolonged survival more effectively than either monotherapy in murine melanoma and colon cancer models. These findings define a TNFα-TNFR2-enhancer axis controlling TIGIT expression and provide a mechanistic rationale for dual TNFα and TIGIT targeting in inflamed tumors.

doi:10.1038/s41388-026-04013-2.abstract: Gastric cancer (GC) is frequently associated with lymph node metastasis, which contributes to a poor prognosis; however, the underlying molecular mechanisms remain incompletely understood. In this study, we identify the N6-methyladenosine (m⁶A) reader IGF2BP1 as a critical driver of lymphatic metastasis in GC. IGF2BP1 is significantly upregulated in GC tissues with lymph node metastasis and is correlated with adverse clinical outcomes. Mechanistically, IGF2BP1 binds to the m⁶A-modified 3' untranslated region (3'UTR) of METTL21A mRNA, thereby enhancing its mRNA stability and expression levels. METTL21A, a non-histone lysine methyltransferase, interacts with and methylates the transcription factor SOX18, facilitating its nuclear translocation without altering protein stability. Once in the nucleus, SOX18 directly activates the transcription of CXCL12. Secreted CXCL12 promotes lymphangiogenesis and facilitates lymphatic metastasis through CXCR4 signaling. Functionally, both IGF2BP1 and METTL21A enhance tube formation and migration of lymphatic endothelial cells and promote lymphatic metastasis in GC. Notably, METTL21A knockout abolishes IGF2BP1-induced lymphangiogenesis, whereas SOX18 depletion eliminates the pro-lymphangiogenic effects of IGF2BP1. Our findings reveal a previously unrecognized signaling axis-IGF2BP1-METTL21A-SOX18-CXCL12-that links m⁶A-dependent post-transcriptional regulation with methylation-dependent transcriptional activation, offering potential therapeutic targets for the prevention of lymphatic metastasis in gastric cancer.

doi:10.1038/s41388-026-04015-0.abstract: Lung squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC) lacks effective targeted therapies despite frequent hyperactivation of the PI3K/AKT pathway, and the contribution of adaptor proteins to this process remains poorly defined. Here, we identify Insulin Receptor Substrate 4 (IRS4) as a common substrate of Src kinase and the phosphatase RPTPα, and uncover a previously unrecognized, conserved phosphorylation site at YY111/112 within the IRS4 PH domain. Src-mediated phosphorylation at this site is essential for IRS4-driven proliferation, anchorage-independent growth, and invasiveness in LUSC cells. Mechanistically, phosphorylation at YY111/112 induces conformational rearrangements in IRS4 that enhance the recruitment of the p85β SH2 domain to the YXXM motif of IRS4, thereby promoting AKT activation without altering IRS4 protein stability or subcellular distribution. An IRS4-derived cell-permeable phosphopeptide containing pYY111/112 disrupts the Src-IRS4 interaction and significantly suppresses tumor growth in vivo in a YY111/112-dependent manner. Consistently, YY111/112 phosphorylation is markedly elevated in human LUSC tissues and correlates with advanced disease stages. Collectively, these findings define a Src-IRS4-PI3K/AKT signaling axis and identify YY111/112 as a critical regulatory site of IRS4 and a potential therapeutic vulnerability in LUSC.

doi:10.1038/s41388-026-04017-y.abstract: KRAS is mutated in 30% of all human cancers. Small molecule inhibitors targeting KRAS with distinct mechanisms-of-action and variable specificities have entered the clinic, but their full effect on the RAS signaling network remains unclear. Here, we described the impact of RAS inhibition on the KRAS interactome using Proximity-dependent Biotin Identification. Two inhibitors were used: panRAS-ON, which forms a ternary complex between cyclophilin and RAS in the GTP-bound state; panKRAS-off, which binds to the KRAS switch II pocket. RAS inhibitors were found to significantly alter 16.5% of proteins in proximity to KRAS. Despite their distinct modality, the KRAS inhibitors induced highly correlated changes in the KRAS interactomes. Among KRAS-proximal proteins, Afadin was highly affected by RAS inhibition. AFDN is a key regulator of cell motility, invasion, and metastasis. Analysis of AFDN phosphorylation revealed that AKT only partially modulates p-Ser1718, while KRAS inhibition sufficiently abolished EGF-mediated AFDN phosphorylation. Silencing AFDN in a KRAS-driven non-small cell lung cancer model abolished chemotaxis and disrupted directional migration in an EGF-driven wound healing model. We demonstrated that KRAS is a central node in regulating growth factor-induced cell migration, and that KRAS inhibition plays a broader role than MAPK-mediated cell proliferation and survival.

doi:10.1038/s41388-026-04018-x.abstract: Therapeutic efficacy of temozolomide (TMZ) remains limited, and GBM patients generally experience poor outcomes due to the presence of multiple mechanisms of TMZ resistance. Previously, we developed two novel compounds: EPIC-1027, which targets HOTAIR/PRC2 complex, and EPIC-1042, which disrupts interaction between PTRF and CAV1. In this study, we aim to establish a novel combinatorial strategy for GBM by targeting mitochondrial function. Proteomics was employed to evaluate global protein alterations induced by EPIC-1027 and EPIC-1042. Super-resolution microscopy and transmission electron microscopy were used to characterize changes in mitochondrial morphology. Metabolic flux analysis was performed to assess alterations in cellular energy metabolism following combined treatment. An intracranial GBM model was established to validate the anti-GBM efficacy of EPIC-1027 and EPIC-1042 in vivo. Combined treatment with EPIC-1027 and EPIC-1042 reduced the abundance of respiratory chain complex proteins by promoting p62-dependent protein degradation, resulting in severe mitochondrial damage. Both glycolytic activity and oxidative phosphorylation were markedly suppressed following EPIC-1027 and EPIC-1042 treatment. In vitro, EPIC-1027 and EPIC-1042 exerted a synergistic inhibitory effect on GBM cell proliferation and significantly induced apoptosis in an MGMT-independent manner. In vivo, combined treatment with EPIC-1027 and EPIC-1042 significantly attenuated tumor growth and prolonged survival in mice bearing orthotopic GBM. Our study demonstrates that combined treatment with EPIC-1027 and EPIC-1042 induces mitochondrial structural abnormalities and functional impairment, leading to suppressed proliferation and enhanced apoptosis. These findings identified a novel combinatorial therapeutic strategy targeting mitochondria for the treatment of glioblastoma.

doi:10.1038/s41388-026-04019-w.abstract: Endocytosis regulates receptor trafficking and signaling, yet its role in colorectal cancer (CRC) remains unclear. We analyzed transcriptomic data from 15,025 CRC tumors to evaluate gene expression in clathrin-mediated endocytosis (CME) and the endosomal sorting complexes required for transport (ESCRT) pathway. Pathway-level signatures were compared across consensus molecular subtypes (CMS) and examined in relation to oncogenic signaling programs, while individual endocytosis-related genes were evaluated for associations with clinical outcomes in an independent randomized trial cohort. Expression of CME and ESCRT pathways varied by CMS, with the highest expression in CMS4 and the lowest in CMS3. Endocytosis signatures correlated with multiple oncogenic signaling pathways, including MAPK, TGF-β, WNT, PI3K, NOTCH, and angiogenesis, suggesting broad links between endocytic activity and tumor biology. In the randomized phase III CALGB/SWOG 80405 trial, low expression of AP2M1-a core adaptor in the CME complex-was significantly associated with longer overall survival and progression-free survival in patients treated with anti-EGFR agents, but not in those receiving anti-VEGF agents. These findings suggest that endocytic trafficking may be associated with oncogenic signaling and differential therapeutic benefit in patients with metastatic CRC. The endocytosis pathway reflects biologically relevant heterogeneity in CRC and may help guide therapeutic stratification.

doi:10.1038/s41388-026-04023-0.abstract: The combination immunotherapies, including those with atezolizumab and bevacizumab (Atez/Bev), have become standard therapy for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). However, its efficacy remains limited and reliable biomarkers are lacking. In this study, we analyzed paired tumor and background liver tissues from Atez/Bev-treated HCC patients and found that high programmed cell death-1 (PD-1) expression in CD8+ tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) correlated with therapeutic response independent of etiology. RNA sequencing on the tumor samples revealed that the branched-chain amino acid (BCAA)-related metabolic pathway was enriched in the group with high PD-1 expression in CD8⁺ TILs. Along with in vitro experiments, we identified the importance of BCAAs for activation and differentiation of CD8+ T cells. In addition, BCAA metabolism was related to response to PD-1 blockade in not subcutaneous but intrahepatic mouse model-specific manner. Actually, public dataset analyses revealed that high expression of BCAT1, a key enzyme in BCAA metabolism, was associated with poor prognosis in HCC, but not in other cancer types. These findings suggest the importance of liver-specific BCAA metabolism in antitumor immunity and highlight the need to assess the tumor microenvironment within its organ-specific metabolic context.

doi:10.1038/s41392-026-02689-2.abstract: Targeted therapy has revolutionized the treatment of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients harboring oncogenic alterations, and next-generation tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) significantly increase blood-brain barrier (BBB) penetration, leading to improved disease control and survival benefits. However, several issues remain to be addressed, including the selection of more appropriate and individualized agents, the emergence of TKI resistance, and the challenging management of central nervous system (CNS) progression. In this review, we comprehensively summarize the efficacy and safety of TKIs and targeted specific antibodies in advanced or metastatic patients with common or rare mutations, providing guidance in selecting the optimal agent. We further explore the mechanisms underlying drug resistance and regimens aimed at overcoming resistance. In nonmetastatic resectable or unresectable NSCLC, we discuss the therapeutic potential of targeted agents and current issues requiring further research. In addition, we distinguish current and potential therapeutic strategies for patients with baseline brain metastasis (BM) and those without baseline BM who subsequently develop brain progression, leading to more effective and personalized treatment. Finally, we provide perspectives on challenges and future directions in the identification and treatment of oncogenic alterations, particularly in the context of co-mutations and the heterogeneous nature of metastases, and emphasize the clinical importance of artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted genetic testing and biomarker development.

doi:10.1038/s41392-026-02786-2.abstract: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is an interstitial lung disease that advances over time and is ultimately life-threatening. Despite advances in antifibrotic therapies, disease progression remains largely unavoidable, highlighting the necessity for advancing mechanistic research and identifying new therapeutic options. Bone morphogenetic protein receptor 2 (BMPR2) is a key receptor for BMP signaling and exerts potent antifibrotic role in lung fibrosis; however, the molecular mechanisms regulating BMPR2 protein stability in fibrotic lungs remain poorly understood. In this study, we identify that the E3 ubiquitin ligase neural precursor cell expressed developmentally downregulated protein 4-like (Nedd4L) as a critical regulator of BMPR2 stability in lung fibroblasts. BMPR2 levels are markedly reduced in lung fibroblasts derived from patients with IPF and in lung tissues from experimental lung fibrosis models. Mechanically, elevated lipid peroxidation in fibrotic lungs induces K48-linked ubiquitination of BMPR2, leading to its degradation and attenuation of BMPs-induced Smad1/5 phosphorylation. Notably, Nedd4L overexpression counteracts lipid peroxidation-induced BMPR2 degradation and promotes BMPs/BMPR2 signaling by shifting BMPR2 ubiquitination toward a stabilizing K63-linked polyubiquitination in lung fibroblasts. We further show that Nedd4L is regulated through threonine phosphorylated by Raf1 kinase in response to increased lipid peroxidation. In vivo, fibroblast-Nedd4L-deficient mice exacerbates experimental lung fibrosis, which is significantly alleviated by BMPR2 overexpression. Collectively, our findings reveal a previously unrecoganized regulatory mechanism of BMPR2 degradation in fibrotic lungs and indicate that stabilizing BMPR2 in lung fibroblasts may represent a promising approach for the treatment of lung fibrosis.

doi:10.1038/s41392-026-02812-3.abstract: Eukaryotic cells contain various membrane- and non-membrane-bound organelles, whose spatial and functional organization underpins intracellular homeostasis. Organelle coordination is governed by complex signaling and metabolic networks, often facilitated by direct physical contacts and molecular exchange. Mitochondria, as central hubs of bioenergetic and metabolic activity, are essential to functional coordination among cellular organelles. They engage in diverse cellular processes, encompassing ATP production, biosynthesis of key metabolites, calcium ion buffering, redox balance, and cellular turnover. To preserve their integrity and functionality, dysfunctional mitochondria undergo selective elimination via mitophagy, a specialized form of macroautophagy. Mitophagy plays dual roles in maintaining mitochondrial fidelity and actively shapes interorganelle communication. Through bidirectional signaling, mitophagy influences the activity of multiple organelles, including the endoplasmic reticulum, nucleus, lysosomes, peroxisomes, and lipid droplets. This interorganelle crosstalk is essential for adapting to metabolic stress, maintaining redox balance, and coordinating cell fate decisions. In this review, we explore the intricate signaling networks connecting mitophagy with various organelles and discuss how these interactions influence organ function and overall cellular health. We also highlight emerging small-molecule modulators of mitophagy, providing insight into potential therapeutic strategies aimed at restoring or enhancing organelle communication in pathological conditions.

doi:10.1038/s41392-026-02840-z.abstract: Receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs), constituting a major family of cell-surface transmembrane receptors, are essential for intracellular tyrosine phosphorylation and signal transduction. RTK signaling is crucial for cellular fate regulation and tissue homeostasis, and its disruption is linked to numerous diseases. Herein, we present a comprehensive review of signaling pathways involving RTKs, with a focus on their signal transduction mechanisms and key components, along with their interactions with major signaling cascades such as G protein-coupled receptors, Wnt, and transforming growth factor β pathways. We also elucidate the multidimensional roles of RTKs in cancer development and progression, highlighting their key effects on cancer stem cell maintenance, tumor microenvironment modulation, and other factors. Furthermore, we systematically summarize the roles of RTKs in noncancerous diseases, including cardiovascular disorders, neurodegenerative diseases, metabolic syndrome, autoimmune conditions, and fibrotic disorders. We then examine current RTK-targeted therapeutics, including small-molecule inhibitors and monoclonal antibodies, for the treatment of various cancers. Finally, novel therapeutic strategies, along with the challenges associated with their development and application, are discussed. In summary, this review will enhance the understanding of the mechanistic aspects of RTK signaling in major disease pathways and provide a detailed overview of recent advancements in targeted therapeutic interventions.

doi:10.1038/s41392-026-02869-0.abstract: Diabetic foot infection (DFI) significantly increases the risks of hospitalization and amputation, with biofilm infections caused by methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) and carbapenem-resistant Escherichia coli (CREC) being key drivers of treatment failure. Here, we analyzed MRSA/CREC biofilm-infected ulcer tissues from patients using proteomics and metabolomics. Compared with nonhealing tissues, healed tissues exhibit activation of low-density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR)-mediated low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) endocytosis and increased free fatty acid production; thus, we hypothesize a potential countermeasure against biofilms. However, the oxidative instability of free fatty acids limits their therapeutic use. Building on our findings demonstrating the potent anti-MRSA/CREC activity of rhein and its synergy with Ag⁺, we developed an injectable hydrogel for sustained codelivery of both agents. This formulation outperforms Ag⁺ monotherapy, accelerating wound closure in biofilm-infected diabetic wounds. Mechanistically, rhein binds to LDLR, upregulates its expression, and enhances the LDL-C endocytosis pathway in vascular endothelial cells to generate more free fatty acids. Among these, eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) is identified as the most critical free fatty acid that promotes healing, as it inhibits biofilm formation and synergizes with Ag⁺ to exert antibacterial and pro-healing effects. In summary, this study identifies endogenous host lipid metabolites as "metabolic antibiotics" and establishes a synergistic therapeutic strategy that concurrently suppresses biofilm formation, inhibits planktonic bacteria, alleviates inflammation, and promotes tissue repair in drug-resistant biofilm-infected diabetic wounds.

doi:10.1038/s41392-026-02869-0.title: Rhein-induced free fatty acid generation cooperates with silver ions for biofilm-infected diabetic wound healing.

doi:10.1038/s41392-026-02876-1.abstract: Liver-organotropic metastasis occurs in cancers such as uveal melanoma (UM) and pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) and is a leading cause of mortality at the terminal stage. Colonization is a rate-limiting and converging step in the metastatic cascade. The drivers underlying liver colonization have largely remained elusive. In this report, we hypothesized that pioneer transcription factors (TFs) increase chromatin accessibility and superenhancer (SE) remodeling, which subsequently promote colonization-associated cellular features [e.g., proliferation, survival, cancer stem cells (CSCs), motility] by driving the transcription of the respective SE-associated genes. We tested this hypothesis and discovered that the pioneer TF KLF4 promoted chromatin accessibility and SE remodeling by ATAC-seq and ChIP-seq. Chromatin accessibility and SE remodeling significantly increased the transcription of the SE-associated genes MCL1 and RASGRP3, which consequently promoted proliferation, motility, and metastasis. Furthermore, the upregulation of KLF4 expression in UM cells was promoted by RN7SL2-containing exosomes from surrounding endothelial cells. Analysis of clinical datasets revealed that the overexpression of RIG-I, STAT1, KLF4, and RASGRP3 was individually correlated with shorter metastasis-free survival or overall survival in patients with UM and PDAC. In conclusion, the identification of the exoRN7SL2-STAT1-KLF4-SEs-RASGRP3 signaling axis may help elucidate metastatic colonization through interactions between tumor cells and the endothelial niche and may yield novel and viable therapeutic targets.

doi:10.1038/s41392-026-02886-z.abstract: Hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) is a chronic inflammatory skin disorder with a high unmet need, particularly for treatment-resistant tunnels. Integrated multiomics analysis revealed that HS tunnels are spatially organized, self-amplifying inflammatory circuits driven by synergistic IL-17/IL-36γ activation of a unique keratinocyte subset, which activates neutrophils and inflammatory fibroblasts. This mechanistic insight coupled with spatial coenrichment of IL-17A and IL-36R provided the rationale for HB0043, a bispecific antibody that leverages IL-36R binding to locally dual-block both cytokines. HB0043 outperformed IL-17A/IL-17F bispecific and parental antibodies in vitro. In a proof-of-concept trial (NCT06895499) involving severe, tunnel-dominant Hurley Stage III HS patients, HB0043 induced promising clinical responses. At week 16, patients demonstrated an 82.13% mean percentage reduction from baseline in total abscess and inflammatory nodule count (AN), while 100% and 80% achieved HiSCR50 and HiSCR75, respectively, alongside ultrasound-confirmed tunnel regression and no major short-term safety signals. Longitudinal plasma proteomics showed suppressed inflammation and restored metabolic homeostasis. By tracking these dynamic systemic alterations alongside local structural changes, our multiomics approach bridges the gap between focal tissue lesions and global systemic disease activity. These findings establish dual blockade of IL-17A and IL-36R as a potential therapeutic strategy, offering a targeted strategy for recalcitrant disease that effectively improves the anatomical therapeutic barriers of advanced hidradenitis suppurativa, thereby demonstrating that cross-pathway bispecific antibodies can dismantle complex inflammatory circuits to achieve structural tissue healing where traditional monotherapies consistently fail.

doi:10.1038/s41392-026-02888-x.abstract: The lack of tumor-specific targeting by oncolytic viruses (OVs) restricts their therapeutic potential. Here, we report a "cap-linker" strategy to modify the vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV) glycoprotein (G protein, VSV-GIN). The modified VSV (Pro-VSVIN) loses its ability to infect cells until present in the tumor microenvironment, where the linker is cleaved by tumor-enriched matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs). When Pro-VSVIN is armed with a single-chain IL-12 (Pro-VSVIN-IL-12) and systemically injected into MC38 tumor-bearing mice, Pro-VSVIN-IL-12 eradicates established tumors while avoiding systemic toxicity, and elicits long-term anti-tumor immune memory. Systemic administration of Pro-VSVIN-IL-12 also markedly inhibits the growth of metastatic cancers in the lung. The efficacy of Pro-VSVIN-IL-12 was further improved when combined with PD-1 checkpoint blockade. Compared to WT VSVIN that carries IL-12, intravenously injected Pro-VSVIN-IL-12 leads to strong Th1 immunity, near abolishment of regulatory T cells, and potent CD8+ T cell activation and clonal expansion in tumors. This preclinical work demonstrates a new tumor-specific targeting strategy of VSV for enhanced immunotherapy safety with superior efficacy.

doi:10.1038/s41392-026-02899-8.abstract: The addition of entinostat, a histone deacetylase inhibitor, to exemestane has demonstrated improved progression-free survival (PFS) in hormone receptor-positive (HR + ), human epidermal growth factor receptor 2-negative (HER2-) advanced breast cancer (ABC) following endocrine therapy failure in the EOC103A3101 randomized trial (NCT03538171). This study reports long-term overall survival (OS) results. In this study, 354 patients with HR + /HER2- ABC that had recurred or progressed after endocrine therapy were randomized (2:1) to receive entinostat plus exemestane (n = 235) or placebo plus exemestane (n = 119). After a median follow-up of 31.8 months, the median OS was 38.6 months (95% confidence interval [CI]: 29.6-44.0) in the entinostat-exemestane group versus 29.2 months (95% CI: 22.5-41.6) in the placebo-exemestane group (hazard ratio [HR] 0.83, 95% CI: 0.62-1.10, P = 0.184). The entinostat-exemestane group demonstrated more pronounced OS benefits when adjusting subsequent antitumor therapies such as cyclin-dependent kinase 4/6 (CDK4/6) inhibitors, or the combination of endocrine therapy, CDK4/6 inhibitors, and chemotherapy. The sensitivity analysis based on the per-protocol set showed more significant OS benefits. The median time to post-discontinuation chemotherapy and chemotherapy-free survival in the entinostat-exemestane group were 11.7 and 9.3 months, respectively, compared to 6.8 and 5.6 months in the placebo-exemestane group (both P < 0.05). Grade ≥3 treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 65.5% of patients in the entinostat-exemestane group, without new safety signals observed. In conclusion, among patients with HR + /HER2- ABC after endocrine therapy failure, entinostat plus exemestane was associated with a numerically longer OS, with an acceptable safety profile.

doi:10.1038/s41392-026-02905-z.abstract: Free radicals are highly reactive molecules that are ubiquitous in aerobic organisms. Among them, oxyradicals like superoxide (O2•-), hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), and hydroxyl radical (OH•), collectively called reactive oxygen species (ROS), have drawn the most attention from researchers in the life sciences and biomedicine because these are the byproducts of aerobic metabolism that are responsible for the oxidative burden experienced by mammalian cells. However, it is now known this oxidative stress only occurs when cells are overwhelmed with ROS and that controlled bursts in free radical production orchestrate signaling pathways essential for organismal health. ROS like H2O2 is now a well-characterized second messenger that transmits signals through protein sulfur switches to activate cell stress coping strategies and induce pathways involved in proliferation, growth, and development. Additionally, defects in these redox systems have been found to be related to many diseases, which has led to the development of new therapeutic modalities to treat and prevent various disorders. In this Review, I will discuss the history of the Redox Biology and Medicine field and how these findings led to the discovery of the three known H2O2 signaling pathways that occur in cells; the floodgate, redox relay, and S-glutathionylation signaling mechanisms. Using this information and new findings generated with advanced molecular biology techniques that have quantified the cellular distance traveled by H2O2, I then propose that cells use these three redox signaling mechanisms to sense and transmit H2O2 signals over short and long cellular distances in mammalian cells.

doi:10.1038/s41392-026-02911-1.abstract: Natural killer (NK) cells have emerged as central players in cancer immunotherapy, progressing from basic discovery to clinically validated platforms over five decades. This review synthesizes the evolving understanding of NK cell biology, including subset heterogeneity, epigenetic regulation, and metabolic control, and, as innovative focal points, intratumoral NK heterogeneity, epigenetic modulation, and intracellular immune checkpoints, forming the foundation for rational therapeutic engineering. We examine the clinical trajectory from unmodified adoptive transfer to cytokine-induced memory-like NK cells and, most transformatively, to chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-NK cells. Landmark trials have established the remarkable efficacy and superior safety of CAR-NK cells in B-cell malignancies, with recent studies extending these benefits to autoimmune diseases such as systemic lupus erythematosus and systemic sclerosis, demonstrating durable immune reset with a favorable safety profile. Despite these advances, solid tumors remain formidable challenges, hindered by antigen heterogeneity, physical barriers, and a metabolically hostile microenvironment. We therefore analyze next-generation engineering strategies that move beyond single modifications toward systems-level reprogramming, encompassing intrinsic enhancements (cytokine signaling, metabolic fitness, checkpoint disruption), extrinsic tumor microenvironment remodeling, and advanced delivery platforms. We further synthesize the practical dimensions of clinical translation by systematically examining key optimization parameters that will guide the path toward precision NK cell therapy. These include rational dosing and scheduling regimens, strategies to reduce lymphodepletion intensity, context-dependent persistence requirements across different disease indications and the emerging biomarker landscape.

doi:10.1038/s41392-026-02921-z.abstract: Anxiety disorders affect more than one-quarter of the global population, but current first-line therapies suffer from slow onset and limited efficacy, highlighting the urgent need for novel pathogenic targets. Psychological stress disrupts iron homeostasis in the brain and alters neural circuit excitability; however, the mechanism underlying these two processes remains elusive. Here, we identify a cell type-specific iron signaling pathway between neurons and astrocytes that mediates stress-induced anxiety by regulating synaptic iron transport in the ventral hippocampal-medial prefrontal cortex circuit. In a chronic restraint stress model in male mice, stress induces activity-dependent HMGB1 expression and release from medial prefrontal cortex pyramidal neurons, which bind to astrocytic TLR4 to stimulate local hepcidin secretion. Hepcidin degrades ferroportin at ventral hippocampal-medial prefrontal cortex axonal terminals in a retrograde manner, blocking presynaptic iron efflux. The resultant iron accumulation in ventral hippocampal-medial prefrontal cortex projection neurons increases their intrinsic excitability via a ferroplasticity mechanism and anxiety-like behaviors. Notably, intranasal administration of HMGB1/TLR4 antagonists efficiently restored synaptic iron flux and alleviated anxiety in both stress-induced and innate high-anxiety models. Collectively, our findings define a retrograde ferrosynaptic neuroglial coupling mechanism through which stress induces anxiety independently of classical synaptic transmission. This work establishes the HMGB1-TLR4-hepcidin-FPN axis as a druggable therapeutic target and provides a conceptual framework for understanding how iron metabolism operates as a transcellular social coordination system in emotional regulation.

doi:10.1038/s41392-026-02926-8.abstract: Ifupinostat (BEBT-908) is a novel dual-targeted inhibitor of histone deacetylase (HDACs) and phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase alpha (PI3Kα). We evaluated the efficacy and safety of ifupinostat monotherapy in patients with relapsed or refractory (r/r) diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) after at least 2 prior lines of systemic therapy. Eligible participants received intravenous ifupinostat at 22.5 mg/m² on days 1, 3, 5, 8, 10, and 12 of a 21-day cycle. The primary endpoint was objective response rate (ORR) assessed by blinded independent central review (BICR). Secondary endpoints included disease control rate (DCR), duration of response (DoR), progression-free survival (PFS), overall survival (OS) and safety. From June 2020 to July 2022, 128 patients were enrolled and included in the safety set (SS), and 115 patients were in the efficacy analysis set (EAS). At the data cutoff (July 2023), the median follow-up was 19.58 months (95% confidence interval [CI] 16.82-21.95). The ORR was 36.5% (42/115, 95% CI 27.7-46.0), with a complete response rate of 11.3% (13/115). The median DoR was 6.2 months (95% CI 3.5-14.5), median PFS was 2.7 months (95% CI 1.6-3.7), and median OS was 9.9 months (95% CI 7.8-14.8). Treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs) occurred in 99.2% (127/128) of patients, and ≥grade 3 TRAEs in 86.7% (111/128). The most common ≥grade 3 TRAEs were thrombocytopenia (75.8%, 97/128), neutropenia (33.6%, 43/128), and leukopenia (22.7%, 29/128). No treatment-related deaths occurred. Ifupinostat demonstrated promising efficacy and a manageable safety profile as a new therapeutic alternative for patients with r/r DLBCL. Clinical Trial Registry Number: ChiCTR1900028179.

doi:10.1038/s41392-026-02931-x.abstract: Pain is a multifaceted sensory and emotional experience that profoundly affects human health and quality of life. It functions as a double-edged sword: while acute pain serves as a protective warning signal, chronic pain compromises physiological and psychological well-being. Pain is now widely regarded as the "fifth vital sign," and given its rising prevalence and substantial global burden, chronic pain may also be considered a major chronic disease entity. Accordingly, elucidating the neural and molecular underpinnings of pain and developing effective analgesic strategies remain urgent priorities. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the molecular and neural circuit mechanisms that govern pain. At the molecular level, ion channels, diverse receptor systems, and intricate signaling pathways play central roles in the transduction and modulation of nociceptive signals. At the circuit level, pain processing involves ascending pathways, descending modulatory systems, and distributed brain regions that collectively encode the sensory and affective dimensions of pain. Building on these mechanistic insights, we discuss current therapeutic strategies, including pharmacological and nonpharmacological interventions, as well as emerging approaches such as gene therapy, stem cell-based therapies and neuromodulation. Despite notable progress, several challenges remain, including the adverse effects associated with existing analgesics and an incomplete understanding of visceral pain mechanisms. Future research should prioritize the integration of multiomics approaches, advanced neural circuit mapping technologies, and artificial intelligence to refine mechanistic insights and enable the development of more precise and effective pain management strategies.

doi:10.1038/s41392-026-02945-5.abstract: Patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus and chronic kidney disease face persistent risks despite standard care. Polyethylene glycol-loxenatide lacks real-world renoprotective evidence in high-risk Chinese populations relative to non-incretin-based standard care. This multicenter, ambispective cohort study enrolled 3305 patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus, renal impairment, and elevated cardiovascular risk at six Chinese tertiary institutions (median follow-up 36.4 months; trial registration: ChiCTR2300073001). Data were extracted via an artificial intelligence-enhanced pipeline. Co-primary analyzes comprised multivariable-adjusted Cox regression and 1:1 propensity score matching (332 per group); pre-specified landmark analyzes at 6 and 12 months addressed immortal time bias. Polyethylene glycol-loxenatide was associated with a reduced risk of the primary kidney composite outcome in the original cohort (hazard ratio [HR], 0.49; 95% CI, 0.25-0.95; P = 0.035), which was corroborated in the propensity score matched cohort (HR, 0.44; 95% CI, 0.20-0.97; P = 0.043) and progressive across 6-month (HR, 0.40; 95% CI, 0.19-0.84) and 12-month (HR, 0.33; 95% CI, 0.14-0.75) landmarks. While a reduction in 3-point major adverse cardiovascular events was observed in the unmatched cohort (HR, 0.60; 95% CI, 0.43-0.85; P = 0.004), this association was not sustained in the matched analysis (HR, 0.92; 95% CI, 0.57-1.48; P = 0.735). In conclusion, long-term therapy was associated with an attenuated risk of major renal events. Given the null findings in the matched cohort, the cardiovascular observations are exploratory and require randomized confirmation.

doi:10.1038/s41392-026-02952-6.abstract: Pulmonary nodules are highly prevalent in adult human populations, with a substantial proportion representing dormant cancerous lesions. We hypothesized that these pulmonary dormant cancers debilitate in growth owing to the lack of an angiogenic switch in tumors. In this study, we comprehensively investigated the hypothesis that specific pathological triggers can activate this angiogenic switch utilizing severe acute respiratory coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) infection-induced hypoxia as a primary physiological stimulus. Our findings provide compelling experimental evidence demonstrating that SARS-CoV-2 infection induces profound pulmonary hypoxia and severe tissue inflammation in animal models. This microenvironmental disruption markedly upregulates the expression of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 2 (VEGFR2) within lung tissues. The resulting hyperactivation of the downstream VEGF-VEGFR2 signaling pathway effectively drives robust pulmonary neovascularization, a phenomenon frequently documented in clinical observations of COVID-19 patients. Furthermore, employing an established experimental tumor model, we demonstrated that SARS-CoV-2 infection directly accelerates tumor outgrowth via this specific VEGF angiogenesis-dependent cascade. Crucially, the targeted administration of a neutralizing antibody to block VEGF significantly suppressed tumor progression and outgrowth in SARS-CoV-2-infected, tumor-bearing animals. Our data show that the COVID-19-induced hypoxia-VEGF-angiogenesis axis serves as one of the mechanisms for initiating tumor outgrowth in pulmonary tissues.

doi:10.1038/s41392-026-02955-3.abstract: Humoral immunity, a fundamental branch of adaptive immunity, relies on B lymphocytes and the antibodies they produce to eliminate extracellular pathogens and neutralize toxins. The development, activation, and differentiation of B cells are tightly regulated by epigenetic mechanisms-including DNA methylation, histone modifications, chromatin dynamics, RNA modifications, and noncoding RNAs-that modulate gene expression without altering the DNA sequence, orchestrating key events such as V(D)J recombination, class switch recombination, somatic hypermutation, germinal center reactions, and the generation of memory B cells and plasma cells. In this review, we summarize how these five categories of epigenetic regulators-together with their respective writers, erasers, readers, and effectors-including DNMT3A/3B and TET enzymes, histone-modifying enzymes, SWI/SNF and INO80 remodeling complexes, N6-methyladenosine and 5-methylcytosine machineries, and microRNAs and long noncoding RNAs-collectively govern B-cell fate decisions, from early lineage commitment in the bone marrow, through germinal center dynamics, to terminal differentiation into plasma cells or memory B cells. We further examine how aberrant epigenetic programs in B cells contribute to pathogenesis across four major disease categories: B-cell malignancies, metabolic and cardiovascular diseases, autoimmune disorders, and infectious diseases. We also discuss sex-biased epigenetic mechanisms, particularly escape from X-chromosome inactivation, that may underlie the female predominance of autoimmune diseases. Finally, we discuss the therapeutic implications of targeting epigenetic regulators and assess the potential of epigenetic signatures as biomarkers.

doi:10.1038/s41392-026-02964-2.abstract: Acne vulgaris is a widespread chronic inflammatory skin condition particularly affecting the pilosebaceous unit, with its pathogenesis intricately linked to excessive sebum production, abnormal follicular keratinization, overcolonization by Cutibacterium acnes (C. acnes), and dysregulated host immune responses. Beyond its dermatological manifestations, the disorder is frequently associated with psychological comorbidities such as anxiety and depression, significantly impacting patients' quality of life. A genetic predisposition is evident, with associated polymorphisms involving pathways related to sebaceous gland activity, inflammatory regulation, and hormonal metabolism. Interactions among immune cells, including macrophages and dendritic cells, along with underlying molecular mechanisms, further contribute to its pathogenesis. Conventional acne treatments face challenges such as increasing antibiotic resistance and limited patient adherence. As a result, clinical research and practice are increasingly focusing on targeted, mechanism-based precision strategies. Recent advances in targeted biologics and vaccines directed against C. acnes have demonstrated promise in clinical studies, offering new avenues for acne management. This review provides a systematic overview of the epidemiology, risk factors, diagnostic classifications, and comorbidities associated with acne, with a particular focus on contemporary insights into its immunopathogenesis and molecular mechanisms. Additionally, it synthesizes current treatment modalities and explores emerging directions, such as acne vaccines and biologics, to serve as a reference for further mechanistic investigation and therapeutic advancement.

doi:10.1038/s41392-026-02965-1.abstract: Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) exhibit remarkable functional heterogeneity, with conserved subtypes observed across diverse malignancies. However, their shared roles in shaping the tumor microenvironment (TME) and their dynamic plasticity remain incompletely understood. In this study, through integrated single-cell and spatial transcriptomic profiling across four cancer types, we identified two distinct immunomodulatory CAF states, termed antigen-presenting CAFs (apCAFs) and matrix-producing CAFs (mCAFs). Across multiple solid tumors, apCAFs were associated with enhanced anti-tumor immune features and favorable prognosis, whereas mCAFs were associated with immunosuppressive characteristics and poorer clinical outcomes. Spatial analyses revealed distinct localization patterns of apCAFs and mCAFs within the TME. Functionally, patient-derived apCAFs promoted T-cell migration, proliferation, and activation, whereas mCAFs suppressed these responses in vitro. Pan-cancer analyses further revealed a strong inverse correlation between apCAF and mCAF abundance across tumor tissues. Mechanistically, IFN-γ and TGF-β-associated signaling contexts were linked to distinct CAF transcriptional programs, with IFN-γ promoting apCAF-associated features and TGF-β favoring mCAF-associated features, suggesting a potential role of cytokine context in shaping CAF state heterogeneity. Clinically, apCAFs correlated with favorable immunotherapy response, whereas mCAFs predicted poor therapeutic outcomes. Collectively, these findings identify conserved immunomodulatory CAF subtypes across cancers, reveal distinct cytokine-associated CAF programs, and support stromal reprogramming as a promising strategy to enhance immunotherapy efficacy.

doi:10.1038/s41392-026-02984-y.abstract: Definitive chemoradiotherapy followed by immunotherapy consolidation is the current standard of care for limited-stage small cell lung cancer (LS-SCLC). We conducted a randomized phase II trial (ChiCTR2000032275) to evaluate a camrelizumab-based induction-consolidation strategy in previously untreated patients with LS-SCLC. Patients were randomly assigned (1:1) to receive induction camrelizumab plus etoposide-platinum followed by concurrent chemoradiotherapy (CRT) and camrelizumab consolidation (camrelizumab group), or induction chemotherapy followed by concurrent CRT alone (cCRT group). The primary endpoint was the 1‑year progression‑free survival (PFS) rate. Secondary endpoints included objective response rate (ORR), PFS, overall survival (OS), and safety. Between November 2020 and April 2024, 41 patients were enrolled. At a median follow‑up of 32.1 months (interquartile range [IQR]: 26.4-38.7), ORR was 100% in the camrelizumab group and 83.3% in the cCRT group. The 1‑year PFS rates were 65.5% with camrelizumab versus 47.4% with cCRT (P = 0.029). Median PFS was 24.0 months versus 11.8 months, and median OS was not reached versus 23.9 months (P = 0.042). Exploratory biomarker analyses indicated that patients with lower baseline systemic inflammatory indices, including neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio <2.8 and platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio <207.0, and those with a decline in lactate dehydrogenase at week 12 after CRT, derived greater benefit from camrelizumab. The OS benefit was also more evident in patients with Ki-67 ≤80%. Toxicities in the camrelizumab group were manageable, with a low incidence of severe immune-related adverse events (4.8%), and radiation pneumonitis rates were comparable between groups. Taken together, induction camrelizumab combined with chemotherapy, followed by CRT and camrelizumab consolidation, significantly improved survival outcomes in LS-SCLC, with a manageable safety profile, warranting further validation for this aggressive malignancy.

doi:10.1038/s41392-026-03103-7.abstract: Pulmonary nodules are increasingly detected by thoracic imaging and low-dose computed tomography-based lung cancer screening, but most are benign, transient, or indolent. Clinically, the key task is to distinguish nodules that require timely cancer-directed evaluation from those that can be safely observed. This review summarizes the classification, disease spectrum, risk assessment, early diagnosis, biomarkers, signaling mechanisms, translational models, and management of pulmonary nodules. We first distinguish imaging phenotypes and disease entities, then differentiate the individual-level models used to select candidates for lung cancer screening from the nodule-level models and structured reporting systems used after nodule detection. Low-dose computed tomography remains the foundation of screening and surveillance approaches, whereas magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), positron emission tomography combined with computed tomography, contrast-enhanced computed tomography, nonsurgical biopsy, surgical diagnosis, and local therapies play more selective roles depending on the probability of malignancy and patient fitness. Noninvasive biomarkers, including circulating cellular, nucleic acid, methylation, protein, autoantibody, extracellular vesicle, and metabolic analytes, are most likely to serve as adjuncts to imaging and clinical risk assessment rather than as stand-alone diagnostic tests. Artificial intelligence may support detection, workflow efficiency, malignancy risk reclassification, invasiveness assessment, and multimodal integration, but its value depends on external validation, calibration, implementation, and prospective evidence of management benefit. Mechanistic studies of adenocarcinoma spectrum subsolid nodules have implicated the involvement of early oncogenic signaling, genomic instability, immune escape, stromal and vascular remodeling, and adaptive survival pathways. Translational models can support mechanistic and procedural research, but do not replicate real-world nodule management in patients. Overall, care for pulmonary nodules should be risk-adapted, longitudinal, multidisciplinary, and patient-centered.

doi:10.1038/s41416-020-01074-2.abstract: Abstract Background Recurrent and/or metastatic squamous cell carcinoma of head and neck (R/M SCCHN) is a common cancer with high recurrence and mortality. Current treatments have low response rates (RRs). Methods Fifty-three patients with R/M SCCHN received continuous oral buparlisib. In parallel, patient-derived xenografts (PDXs) were established in mice to evaluate resistance mechanisms and efficacy of buparlisib/cetuximab combination. Baseline and on-treatment tumour genomes and transcriptomes were sequenced. Based on the integrated clinical and PDX data, 11 patients with progression under buparlisib monotherapy were treated with a combination of buparlisib and cetuximab. Results For buparlisib monotherapy, disease control rate (DCR) was 49%, RR was 3% and median progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) were 63 and 143 days, respectively. For combination therapy, DCR was 91%, RR was 18% and median PFS and OS were 111 and 206 days, respectively. Four PDX models were originated from patients enrolled in the current clinical trial. While buparlisib alone did not inhibit tumour growth, combination therapy achieved tumour inhibition in three of seven PDXs. Genes associated with apoptosis and cell-cycle arrest were expressed at higher levels with combination treatment than with buparlisib or cetuximab alone. Conclusions The buparlisib/cetuximab combination has significant promise as a treatment strategy for R/M SCCHN. Clinical Trial Registration NCT01527877.

doi:10.1038/s41416-026-03630-8.abstract: In Head and Neck Cancer (HNC), even short delays in treatment can worsen prognosis. We used real-world data to quantify waiting times and identify patient, tumour and health service factors associated with treatment delay in England. Using linked national datasets (Cancer Registry, Cancer Waiting Times, Hospital Episodes Statistics, Radiotherapy and Chemotherapy), we calculated waiting times from referral to first treatment (surgery or (chemo)radiation) and used multivariable logistic regression models to examine factors associated with delay. Of 30,506 patients, 43% experienced treatment delay ( > 62 days from referral). Long delays ( > 90 days) affected 11% of patients treated with primary surgery and 20% of those receiving primary (chemo)radiation. Non-urgent referral (30% of patients) was the strongest predictor of long delay (aOR 4.07, CI: 3.54-4.68). Additional risk-factors included initial assessment at non-specialist (spoke) hospitals, non-oropharyngeal cancers, and higher socio-economic deprivation. Treatment delays in HNC are worsening, particularly for patients treated with primary (chemo)radiation. Referral route is the strongest determinant. Interventions should focus on optimising referral pathways, increasing awareness of HNC symptoms among the public and primary care, and acknowledging the different drivers of delay associated with surgery and (chemo)radiation therapy.

doi:10.1038/s41416-026-03631-7.abstract: The sixth Paediatric Therapeutic Development Workshop focused on desmoplastic small round cell tumours (DSRCT). Less than 20% of patients with DSRCT survive beyond 5 years and there is no targeted therapy for this disease, which represents an urgent unmet need for new therapeutics. High priority targets include the EWSR1::WT1 fusion protein, the oncogenic driver, and targeting a junction-derived neopeptide presented by HLA-A*03 and HLA-A*11 using a T-cell receptor (TCR) is a novel approach. Other targets (LRRC15, SSTR3 and SSTR5, NECTIN4, STEAP1 and mesothelin) require further validation. Targeting ERBB2/HER2 or claudin-6 by antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) and NTRK3 by a small molecule inhibitor are promising approaches and are currently being evaluated. Existing clinical assets targeting (in order of importance) B7-H3, the DNA damage response, androgen signalling, FGFR4 and STEAP1 are also high priorities for evaluation in DSRCT, but obtaining therapeutics for clinical trials is a barrier. In view of the rarity of DSRCT, a global initiative in preclinical and clinical research to establish international trials and collect data from patients treated in a harmonised form would benefit patients. Progress can be made by a combined approach of developing new agents whilst evaluating existing therapeutics in well-designed trials.

doi:10.1038/s41416-026-03632-6.abstract: The hypoxic microenvironment, a common feature of solid tumors, is critically involved in driving cancer malignancy. This research focuses on elucidating the function of high mobility group box 1 (HMGB1), induced by such hypoxia, in the context of oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC). We first profiled HMGB1 expression patterns in clinical OSCC specimens and evaluated their potential associations with clinicopathological parameters. To functionally characterize HMGB1, we conducted in vitro experiments utilizing silencing strategies. The impact of chronic cyclic hypoxia and HMGB1 depletion on key cellular processes-including proliferation, pyroptosis, and cell cycle-was systematically examined in OSCC cells. Signaling activity along the HMGB1/NLRP3/Caspase-1 axis was determined by immunoblotting. Furthermore, in vivo relevance was substantiated through murine xenograft models and a 4-NQO-induced carcinogenesis protocol. Analysis of clinical samples revealed that HMGB1 is constitutively upregulated in OSCC tissues. This elevated expression demonstrated a positive relationship with both increased tumor dimensions and lymph node metastasis. Subsequent Kaplan-Meier survival curves indicated that heightened HMGB1 levels are a marker for unfavorable patient outcomes. Furthermore, in cell culture systems, hypoxia treatment significantly elevates HMGB1 expression levels in OSCC cells. Knockdown of HMGB1 expression inhibits hypoxia-induced NLRP3, cleaved-caspase-1, and HIF-1α expression. Hypoxia treatment markedly enhanced OSCC cell proliferation, induced pyroptosis, and alleviated G2/M phase arrest, while HMGB1 knockdown reversed the pro-tumor effects of hypoxia. In vivo experiments demonstrated that HMGB1 knockdown inhibited tumor growth, whereas NLRP3 or caspase-1 deficiency delayed oral cancer progression. Our findings suggested that HMGB1 contributes to the progression of OSCC and has prognostic value. Targeting the hypoxia-induced HMGB1/NLRP3/Caspase-1 signaling axis may offer a viable therapeutic strategy.

doi:10.1038/s41416-026-03634-4.abstract: As potent triggers of innate immunity, STING agonists hold promise as active immunotherapeutic agents for cancer treatment. Second-generation STING agonists, suitable for systemic delivery, are being investigated in preclinical research and have entered clinical trials. Here, the novel synthetic STING agonist, BI-1703880 (STINGa), was investigated for anti-tumour and immunological effects. We used human and murine immune and tumour cells to examine the effects of STINGa in vitro, and preclinical cancer mouse models to investigate effects in vivo. We show that STINGa activates the STING pathway and results in a transient and dose-dependent upregulation and secretion of interferons and proinflammatory cytokines in vitro and in vivo. We show that intravenous administration of repeated dosing with low-dose STINGa is well tolerated. We report that radiotherapy (RT) and STING agonism synergises to generate innate immune cell and CD8+ T cell responses that control tumour growth. RT/STINGa upregulated PD-L1, PD-1 and CTLA-4 in the tumour microenvironment. Our findings show that combining RT/STINGa with immune checkpoint inhibitors further increases therapeutic benefit. Our data confirm STING as a therapeutic target in cancer and support the clinical development of BI1703880 STING agonist, thereby suggesting radiotherapy as a potential combination for enhancing anti-tumour efficacy.

doi:10.1038/s41416-026-03636-2.abstract: The pathogenesis of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) involves chronic inflammation of the gastrointestinal tract, which predisposes patients to an increased risk of fibrosis and cancer due to prolonged inflammatory stimulation. However, the specific mechanisms underlying secondary gastrointestinal carcinogenesis in individuals with IBD remain poorly elucidated, particularly due to a limited number of studies conducted at single-nuclei level. We investigated the dynamics and interactions of cell subtypes during the progression of IBD-associated cancers through comprehensive analysis including single-nuclei transcriptomics, spatial transcriptomics, ecological dynamic modelling, multiplex immunohistochemistry, in vitro co-culture and in vivo animal studies. The results revealed that CXCL14+ fibroblasts, the primary source of collagen in the microenvironment, play a pivotal role in the inflammation-cancer transition. These fibroblasts progressively increase in abundance during this transition and secreted elevated levels of collagen IV. The increased presence of collagen IV promotes the recruitment and differentiation of SPP1+ macrophages. This interaction ultimately contributes to the development and progression of IBD-associated fibrosis and cancer transformation. Collagen IV, secreted by CXCL14+ fibroblasts, plays a pivotal role in promoting the transition from IBD to cancer. Inhibition of collagen IV secretion not only prevents fibrosis but also hinders the development of inflammation-cancer transition. Our findings are crucial for understanding the mechanisms underlying IBD-associated cancer and developing innovative therapeutic strategies. During the inflammation-cancer transition, activation of the SOX4 leads to increased COL4A1/A2 secretion by CXCL14+ fibroblasts, resulting in enhanced collagen IV synthesis. Collagen IV binds to ITGB1/CD44 receptors on SPP1+ macrophages and activates EGR1/2 to promote SPP1+ macrophage differentiation, while upregulating S100A10 and ANXA2. Activation of S100A10 and ANXA2 promotes recruitment of SPP1+ macrophages, which contributes to immune escape and secretion of oncogenes, thus further promoting fibrosis and tumorigenesis. In addition, SPP1+ macrophages further stimulate CXCL14+ fibroblasts to secrete COL4A1/A2 via TGF-β1, forming a feedback loop that amplifies interactions in the tumour microenvironment.

doi:10.1038/s41416-026-03641-5.abstract: The Geriatric Core Dataset (G-CODE) was developed to standardise geriatric assessment (GA) in older adults with cancer. This study aimed to develop and externally validate a mortality prediction score based on the G-CODE at 6-month (main endpoint), 12- and 24-month (secondary endpoints), in older patients with cancer. Data came from two prospective French cohorts of cancer patients aged ≥70 referred for GA: the Elderly Cancer Patients (ELCAPA) cohort (training set) and the Geriatric Oncology Marseille (GOM) cohort (validation set). G-CODE items were evaluated using multivariate Cox regression analyses, with Akaike information criterion selection. Discrimination was assessed using time-dependent area under the receiver operator curve (tAUC) for 6-, 12-, and 24-month mortality. We included 950 and 766 patients in the training and validation sets (mean ± sd age: 83 ± 6 years/81 ± 6 years; men: 55%/59%; 6-month mortality: 27%/22%). The final G-CODE model highlighted five strong predictors of 6-month mortality: not having a caregiver, weight loss, comorbidities, an impaired 4-instrumental activities of daily living score, and an impaired timed-up-and-go test. The tAUCs of the model, including the G-CODE, age, cancer type, metastases, and treatment, were 82%, 78% and 80%. The final G-CODE score (range: 0-17) accurately predicts 6-, 12-, and 24-month mortality. NCT02884375 (ClinicalTrials.gov).
