doi:10.1126/sciadv.aei1213.abstract: The circadian clock enhances plant fitness by aligning internal timing with the external photoperiod, but how it coordinates spatiotemporal regulation with chromatin dynamics to improve salt tolerance is not well understood. Here, we show that the clock component TIME FOR COFFEE (TIC) forms biomolecular condensates in response to salt stress, but not to osmotic stress alone. Consistently, tic mutants were hypersensitive to salt stress yet displayed enhanced salt tolerance under 21-hour light-dark cycles matching their shortened circadian period, highlighting the importance of circadian clock in salt tolerance. Salt stress increases H3K9ac levels at the salt stress-responsive genes and induces their expression in a time-of-day-dependent manner in wild-type plants, whereas both H3K9ac level and transcriptional activation are attenuated in tic mutants. TIC physically associates with HD2-type histone deacetylases, and a subset of HD2 partially colocalizes with TIC condensates in the nucleolus under salt stress. Genetic and biochemical analyses showed that salt stress promotes TIC condensate formation, accompanied by reduced HD2 occupancy at salt stress-responsive loci, thereby elevating H3K9ac levels and promoting gene expression. Together, these findings uncover a mechanism by which salt-induced TIC condensate formation links chromatin regulation with circadian timing, thereby promoting plant adaptation to salt stress.

doi:10.1126/sciadv.aei1336.abstract: Liquid crystal displays (LCDs) use thin pixels of a paraelectric nematic, confined between two glass plates with transparent indium tin oxide (ITO) electrodes. A voltage applied to the electrodes realigns the molecules, changing optical appearance of the pixel. Here, we demonstrate that a similar molecular realignment can be triggered by a low-power light irradiation when the paraelectric nematic in the cell with ITO electrodes is replaced with a ferroelectric nematic (NF). Irradiation creates an intrinsic electric field that is strong enough to realign the NF but too weak to affect the paraelectric nematic. The extraordinary sensitivity of the ITO/NF pair to light irradiation creates a platform for optical control of ferroelectric polarization and applications in photonics, sensing, smart windows, and beyond.

doi:10.1126/sciadv.aei2144.abstract: Ozone has been viewed as the principal oxidant of skin oils and other unsaturated surface films, but their fate under realistic indoor conditions remains poorly constrained. Here, we use squalene (SQ), a major component of skin lipids, to investigate the dominant oxidation pathways in occupied indoor environments and laboratory flow reactors. With exposure to indoor air, SQ decay and reactive oxygen species (ROS) formation accelerated over time, consistent with autoxidation. Laboratory experiments with ozone alone drove first-order SQ loss and humidity-dependent emissions of volatile organic compounds (VOCs). In contrast, exposure to both ozone and •OH produced nonexponential SQ decays, higher ROS yields, a much stronger in-film •OH source, and condensed-phase products enriched in highly oxidized organic hydroperoxides that closely match those observed indoors. Unexpectedly, gas-phase •OH strongly suppressed VOC emissions. These results demonstrate that gas-phase radical-induced autoxidation governs SQ aging, challenging the prevailing ozone-centric view of indoor skin oil oxidation.

doi:10.1126/sciadv.aei3111.abstract: Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) H5N1 virus spillover into dairy cows represents the emergence of a mammalian host capable of sustaining a panzootic and creates a transmission pathway to humans. HPAI research involving dairy cows is constrained by the space requirements needed to house large animals in high biocontainment. A small ruminant model would enable larger sample sizes while reducing costs, improving safety, and lowering logistical barriers to conduct research. Here, we establish dairy goats as a model for HPAI mammary infection. Intramammary inoculation with HPAI H5N1 genotype D1.1 and genotype B3.13 resulted in acute mastitis, decreased milk yield, and high virus shedding in milk. Parenteral vaccination with an inactivated virus induced antigen-specific antibodies in blood and milk, reduced clinical disease, limited virus shedding in milk, and mitigated milk production losses. HPAI H5N1 disease dynamics in dairy cows can be recapitulated in dairy goats, providing a relevant model for investigating pathogenesis and for supporting the development of control strategies.

doi:10.1126/sciadv.aei3285.abstract: The selective oxidation of methane under mild conditions remains a formidable challenge because of the inert C─H bond and the ease of over-oxidation. Here we report a facile strategy that enables methane conversion at room temperature and ambient pressure using molecular O2 and commercially available Cu powder in dilute aqueous H2SO4. The reaction is capable of proceeding with only trace CO2 formation, producing methyl bisulfate and methanol as the primary partial oxidation products. In situ Raman spectroscopy indicates that an in situ O2-derived Cu2O surface is the reaction-relevant phase associated with C─H bond activation. The observed selectivity arises from bisulfate adsorption on this Cu2O surface, which suppresses methanol over-oxidation, together with the interception of surface-generated methyl intermediates to form oxidation-resistant methyl bisulfate. This Cu/O2-H2SO4 system demonstrates that methane can be selectively oxidized under mild aqueous conditions and provides mechanistic insight into Cu/O2-mediated oxidation, suggesting a bisulfate-assisted approach to suppressing over-oxidation that may be applicable to other substrates.

doi:10.1126/sciadv.aei3285.title: Bisulfate-mediated selective methane oxidation under mild aqueous conditions.

doi:10.1126/sciadv.aei5334.abstract: Investigating neural circuits underlying complex behavior requires high-resolution imaging of large neuronal populations during naturalistic conditions. Miniaturized two-photon microscopes (MINI2Ps) enable deep brain imaging in freely moving animals when coupled with gradient index (GRIN)-based microendoscopes. However, intrinsic optical aberrations in GRIN-based microendoscopes degrade spatial resolution and limit the effective field-of-view (FOV). Here, we address these limitations using lightweight microfabricated optics to correct GRIN aberrations during deep brain MINI2P imaging. The aberration corrected system demonstrated improved and more homogeneous axial resolution across the FOV, resulting in more than fourfold increase in effective FOV. We applied the corrected system to the ventral posteromedial thalamus in freely moving mice and performed optical mapping of head direction (HD) tuned cells. These measurements revealed the absence of spatial clustering of HD preference, suggesting spatially sparse HD coding in sensory thalamus. Combining the MINI2P with aberration corrected GRIN-based microendoscopes is a powerful approach for large-scale and high-resolution functional imaging of deep brain circuits during naturalistic behavior.

doi:10.1126/sciadv.aei6572.abstract: Subduction zones govern Earth's deep volatile cycle. The slab-mantle interface is a key locus of volatile exchange between the subducting crust and the overlying mantle wedge, yet whether and how chemical reactions at this interface affect arc magmatism remains poorly constrained. Arc magmas typically lack a geochemical hallmark of garnet fractionation, leading to the prevailing interpretation that they derive predominantly from the shallower, garnet-free mantle wedge. Here, we challenge this view using Mg isotopic data from Nicaragua, the South Sandwich Islands, and the central-eastern Aleutian arc, integrated with a global arc magma compilation. We show that heavy Mg isotopic signatures in mafic arc magmas vary with indicators of volatile enrichment, pointing to a volatile-rich source, most likely the heavily metasomatized base of the mantle wedge. The heaviest Mg isotopic compositions occur in arcs underlain by the most steeply dipping subducting slab, suggesting a focusing effect by the geometry of the downgoing slab. Monte Carlo isotope mixing models indicate that up to 50% of the Mg budget in some arc magma sources derives from deep, water-saturated melting near the slab-mantle interface. These findings highlight the base of the mantle wedge as a volumetrically and geochemically significant contributor to arc magmatism and the water cycle.

doi:10.1126/sciadv.aei9275.abstract: Differences in lithology within alpine watersheds lead to strong contrasts in bedrock erodibility, which modulate climatic and tectonic influences on erosion, chemical weathering, and carbon dioxide exchange. However, the difficulty of measuring denudation rates in fine-grained rocks has limited our ability to quantify the magnitude of erodibility differences between weak sedimentary and strong igneous rocks. Here, we combine newly developed cosmogenic beryllium-10 measurements in shale with conventional beryllium-10 measurements in intrusive rocks, topographic analysis, solute data, and landscape evolution modeling in the East River watershed, Colorado. Shale-dominated catchments denude three times faster than adjacent intrusive catchments despite having gentler topography. Hydrochemical data and modeling indicate that elevated shale denudation enhances solute generation and net inorganic weathering-driven carbon dioxide release during prolonged landscape adjustment over million-year timescales. These results show that spatial variability in rock type alone can substantially alter the carbon dioxide balance of alpine landscapes by hiding the fastest erosion rates in relatively gentle terrain.

doi:10.1126/sciadv.aei9401.abstract: Highly selective oxidation of methane to liquid oxygenates under mild conditions remains challenging because of the difficulty in controlling overoxidation at highly reactive sites. Here, we demonstrate remote control of single-atom Cu reactivity through outer-shell coordination engineering in Zr-based metal-organic frameworks (MOFs). By anchoring Cu1 to Zr-oxo nodes in UiO-66-X (X = -NO2, -H, and -CH3), remote X-BDC ligands systematically modulate the electronic properties of Cu1 sites and the catalytic microenvironment. In situ characterization combined with ab initio molecular dynamics in an explicitly solvated aqueous environment reveals a dynamic outer-shell-to-inner-shell regulation that reshapes the active structure and reactive oxygen species around Cu1 sites, thereby facilitating CH4 activation. In particular, the electron-withdrawing NO2-BDC ligand creates electron-deficient Cu1-•OH* sites, while adsorbed water further regulates active-site conformation. Consequently, Cu1/U6-NO2 achieves a turnover frequency of 322.4 h-1 with nearly 100% oxygenate selectivity under mild conditions, establishing a general strategy for overcoming activity-selectivity trade-offs in methane conversion.

doi:10.1126/sciadv.aei9788.abstract: Escherichia coli couples the initiation of DNA replication with cell size by modulating the activity of the replication initiator protein DnaA. The activity of DnaA is regulated both by its interconversion between an active and inactive form and by its titration on chromosomal binding sites. Whereas its interconversion has been thoroughly studied, the extent to which DnaA titration can control replication initiation is poorly understood. Here, we describe the control of E. coli DNA replication via titration by modulating the expression of a constitutively active DnaA variant in four growth conditions. While we obtained stable cell cycles during slow growth, faster growth associated with overlapping replication forks led to initiation instability and replicative stress. Overall, our results provide insights into the limits of titration-based systems in the control of genome replication and their potential role in the evolutionary trajectory of E. coli. Last, this study provides design principles for a simplified, titration-only regulatory mechanism for DNA replication in synthetic cells.

doi:10.1126/sciadv.aej0353.abstract: The slow kinetics of sulfur cathodes caused by the high energy barriers of Li+ desolvation stem primarily from the structure of the inner Helmholtz plane (IHP). Herein, a synergistic strategy combining electrochemical tandem catalysis with spatial nanoconfinement is proposed to regulate the Li(solvent)x+ dynamics. As a proof-of-concept, the porous covalent organic framework (denoted as TPBD) decorated MXene is in situ constructed, acting as a tandem kinetic promoter. The theoretical simulations and in situ Raman reveal that the porous TPBD layer confines the bulky Li(solvent)x+ species and sieves the spatial structure with accelerated Li+ diffusion kinetics. Meanwhile, MXene serves as a negatively charged substrate that helps disrupt anion-solvent interactions and reconstruct the solvation structure at the IHP, thereby enhancing Li+ kinetics and sulfur redox reversibility. Encouragingly, the assembled cells demonstrate a superior Li+ transference number (0.77), long-term cycling lifespan up to 1000 cycles, as well as excellent areal capacity (>6 mAh cm-2) at 0°C and superior rate capability at 50°C under a high sulfur loading of 7.51 mg cm-2. The as-prepared pouch cell remains stable for over 100 cycles, validating this novel integration of catalysis and nanoconfinement for tandem kinetics in Li-S batteries.

doi:10.1126/sciadv.aej4446.abstract: The global emergence of deep-sea sediments enriched in rare-earth elements and yttrium (REY) after the Late Eocene cooling coincides spatiotemporally with Antarctic bottom water (AABW) expansion, yet the underlying mechanism remains unresolved. Here, we present in situ elemental and neodymium isotopic analyses of apatites extracted from Oligocene-Miocene sediments along the North Pacific AABW pathway. Results show ∼90% of the REY budget resides in inner dentin of fossil teeth. The dentin and coexisting authigenic fluorapatites display similar εNd values (∼-5) matching North Pacific seawater, whereas outer dense layer carries a distinct, less-radiogenic εNd (∼-10) resembling South Pacific seawater. This isotopic decoupling establishes fossil teeth as dual archives: The outer layer preserves the εNd signature of the fish's living environment, while the inner dentin records its depositional environment. We propose that AABW collects, transports, and sorts fossil teeth along its flow path, ultimately leading to the global occurrence of REY-rich sediments in downstream basins.

doi:10.1126/sciadv.aej9757.abstract: The interplay between coherent (wave-like) and incoherent (particle-like) phonon transport is central to heat conduction, yet experimental evidence of their crossover in bulk three-dimensional (3D) crystals remains scarce. Here, we report intrinsically ultralow lattice thermal conductivity ([Formula: see text]) in the lead-free double perovskite Cs2AgBiCl6, reaching 0.52 and 0.28 W m-1 K-1 in single crystal and polycrystals, respectively, at room temperature. Combining thermal transport, low-temperature heat capacity, Raman spectroscopy, synchrotron x-ray pair distribution function analysis, and anharmonic lattice-dynamics calculations, we uncover the microscopic origin of this anomalous heat transport. Chemical bonding heterogeneity, weakly bound rattling-like Cs vibrations, anisotropic Cl dynamics, and soft lattice modes generate low-energy localized optical phonons that strongly interact with acoustic modes. Enhanced three- and four-phonon scattering suppresses phonon lifetimes, while anharmonic renormalization flattens optical branches and reduces group velocities. Coherent contributions account for ∼50% of [Formula: see text] near room temperature and exceeding incoherent contributions above ∼200 K, revealing an emergent coherent-incoherent phonon crossover in a fully crystalline 3D solid.

doi:10.1126/scitranslmed.abn8238.abstract: Increased orexin/hypocretin signaling is implicated in opioid withdrawal, sleep disturbances, and drug-seeking behaviors. This study examined whether a dual-orexin receptor antagonist would improve sleep and withdrawal outcomes when compared with placebo during a buprenorphine/naloxone taper. Thirty-eight participants with opioid use disorder were recruited to a clinical research unit and maintained on 8/2 to 16/4 mg of buprenorphine/naloxone treatment for 3 days before being randomized to 20 mg of suvorexant ( n = 14), 40 mg of suvorexant ( n = 12), or placebo ( n = 12); 26 individuals completed the study. After randomization, participants underwent a 4-day buprenorphine/naloxone taper and 4-day post-taper observation period. Total sleep time (TST) was collected nightly with a wireless electroencephalography device and wrist-worn actigraphy; opioid withdrawal symptoms were assessed via the Subjective Opiate Withdrawal Scale (SOWS); and abuse potential was assessed on a 0- to 100-point visual analog scale of “High” every morning. A priori outcomes included two-group (collapsing suvorexant doses versus placebo) and three-group comparisons of area-under-the-curve (AUC) scores for TST, SOWS, and High. In two-group comparisons, participants receiving suvorexant displayed increased TST during the buprenorphine/naloxone taper and decreased SOWS during the post-taper period. In three-group comparisons, participants receiving 20 mg of suvorexant versus placebo displayed increased AUC for TST during the buprenorphine/naloxone taper, but there was no difference in SOWS among groups. There was no evidence of abuse potential in two- or three-group analyses. The results suggest that suvorexant might be a promising treatment for sleep and opioid withdrawal in individuals undergoing a buprenorphine/naloxone taper.

doi:10.1126/scitranslmed.abp8982.abstract: Precise estimates of epileptogenic zone networks (EZNs) are crucial for planning intervention strategies to treat drug-resistant focal epilepsy. Here, we present the virtual epileptic patient (VEP), a workflow that uses personalized brain models and machine learning methods to estimate EZNs and to aid surgical strategies. The structural scaffold of the patient-specific whole-brain network model is constructed from anatomical T1 and diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging. Each network node is equipped with a mathematical dynamical model to simulate seizure activity. Bayesian inference methods sample and optimize key parameters of the personalized model using functional stereoelectroencephalography recordings of patients’ seizures. These key parameters together with their personalized model determine a given patient’s EZN. Personalized models were further used to predict the outcome of surgical intervention using virtual surgeries. We evaluated the VEP workflow retrospectively using 53 patients with drug-resistant focal epilepsy. VEPs reproduced the clinically defined EZNs with a precision of 0.6, where the physical distance between epileptogenic regions identified by VEP and the clinically defined EZNs was small. Compared with the resected brain regions of 25 patients who underwent surgery, VEP showed lower false discovery rates in seizure-free patients (mean, 0.028) than in non–seizure-free patients (mean, 0.407). VEP is now being evaluated in an ongoing clinical trial (EPINOV) with an expected 356 prospective patients with epilepsy.

doi:10.1126/scitranslmed.abq4433.abstract: Dysregulated host responses to infection can lead to organ dysfunction and sepsis, causing millions of global deaths each year. To alleviate this burden, improved prognostication and biomarkers of response are urgently needed. We investigated the use of whole-blood transcriptomics for stratification of patients with severe infection by integrating data from 3149 samples from patients with sepsis due to community-acquired pneumonia or fecal peritonitis admitted to intensive care and healthy individuals into a gene expression reference map. We used this map to derive a quantitative sepsis response signature (SRSq) score reflective of immune dysfunction and predictive of clinical outcomes, which can be estimated using a 7- or 12-gene signature. Last, we built a machine learning framework, SepstratifieR, to deploy SRSq in adult and pediatric bacterial and viral sepsis, H1N1 influenza, and COVID-19, demonstrating clinically relevant stratification across diseases and revealing some of the physiological alterations linking immune dysregulation to mortality. Our method enables early identification of individuals with dysfunctional immune profiles, bringing us closer to precision medicine in infection.

doi:10.1126/scitranslmed.adg2841.abstract: Troponin I (TnI) regulates thin filament activation and muscle contraction. Two isoforms, TnI-fast ( TNNI2 ) and TnI-slow ( TNNI1 ), are predominantly expressed in fast- and slow-twitch myofibers, respectively. TNNI2 variants are a rare cause of arthrogryposis, whereas TNNI1 variants have not been conclusively established to cause skeletal myopathy. We identified recessive loss-of-function TNNI1 variants as well as dominant gain-of-function TNNI1 variants as a cause of muscle disease, each with distinct physiological consequences and disease mechanisms. We identified three families with biallelic TNNI1 variants (F1: p.R14H/c.190-9G>A, F2 and F3: homozygous p.R14C), resulting in loss of function, manifesting with early-onset progressive muscle weakness and rod formation on histology. We also identified two families with a dominantly acting heterozygous TNNI1 variant (F4: p.R174Q and F5: p.K176del), resulting in gain of function, manifesting with muscle cramping, myalgias, and rod formation in F5. In zebrafish, TnI proteins with either of the missense variants (p.R14H; p.R174Q) incorporated into thin filaments. Molecular dynamics simulations suggested that the loss-of-function p.R14H variant decouples TnI from TnC, which was supported by functional studies showing a reduced force response of sarcomeres to submaximal [Ca 2+ ] in patient myofibers. This contractile deficit could be reversed by a slow skeletal muscle troponin activator. In contrast, patient myofibers with the gain-of-function p.R174Q variant showed an increased force to submaximal [Ca 2+ ], which was reversed by the small-molecule drug mavacamten. Our findings demonstrated that TNNI1 variants can cause muscle disease with variant-specific pathomechanisms, manifesting as either a hypo- or a hypercontractile phenotype, suggesting rational therapeutic strategies for each mechanism.

doi:10.1126/scitranslmed.adh8335.abstract: Labor is a complex physiological process requiring a well-orchestrated dialogue between the mother and fetus. However, the cellular contributions and communications that facilitate maternal-fetal cross-talk in labor have not been fully elucidated. Here, single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) was applied to decipher maternal-fetal signaling in the human placenta during term labor. First, a single-cell atlas of the human placenta was established, demonstrating that maternal and fetal cell types underwent changes in transcriptomic activity during labor. Cell types most affected by labor were fetal stromal and maternal decidual cells in the chorioamniotic membranes (CAMs) and maternal and fetal myeloid cells in the placenta. Cell-cell interaction analyses showed that CAM and placental cell types participated in labor-driven maternal and fetal signaling, including the collagen, C-X-C motif ligand (CXCL), tumor necrosis factor (TNF), galectin, and interleukin-6 (IL-6) pathways. Integration of scRNA-seq data with publicly available bulk transcriptomic data showed that placenta-derived scRNA-seq signatures could be monitored in the maternal circulation throughout gestation and in labor. Moreover, comparative analysis revealed that placenta-derived signatures in term labor were mirrored by those in spontaneous preterm labor and birth. Furthermore, we demonstrated that early in gestation, labor-specific, placenta-derived signatures could be detected in the circulation of women destined to undergo spontaneous preterm birth, with either intact or prelabor ruptured membranes. Collectively, our findings provide insight into the maternal-fetal cross-talk of human parturition and suggest that placenta-derived single-cell signatures can aid in the development of noninvasive biomarkers for the prediction of preterm birth.

doi:10.1126/scitranslmed.adi0178.abstract: Perineural invasion (PNI) is a biological characteristic commonly observed in pancreatic cancer. Although PNI plays a key role in pancreatic cancer metastasis, recurrence, and poor postoperative survival, its mechanism is largely unclarified. Clinical sample analysis and endoscopic ultrasonographic elasticity scoring indicated that cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) were closely related to the occurrence of PNI. Furthermore, CAF-derived extracellular vesicles (EVs) were involved in PNI in dorsal root ganglion coculture and mouse sciatic nerve models. Next, we demonstrated that CAFs promoted PNI through extracellular vesicle transmission of PNI-associated transcript (PIAT). Mechanistically, PIAT specifically bound to YBX1 and blocked the YBX1-Nedd4l interaction to inhibit YBX1 ubiquitination and degradation. Furthermore, PIAT enhanced the binding of YBX1 and PNI-associated mRNAs in a 5-methylcytosine (m5C)–dependent manner. Mutation of m5C recognition motifs in YBX1 or m5C sites in downstream target genes reversed PIAT-mediated PNI. Consistent with these findings, analyses using a KPC mouse model demonstrated that the PIAT/YBX1 axis enhanced PNI through m5C modification. Clinical data suggested that the PIAT expression in the serum EVs of patients with pancreatic cancer was associated with the degree of neural invasion and prognosis. Our study revealed the important role of the PIAT/YBX1 signaling axis in the tumor microenvironment (TME) in promoting tumor cell PNI and provided a new target for precise interference with CAFs and RNA methylation in the TME to suppress PNI in pancreatic cancer.

doi:10.1126/scitranslmed.adi3363.abstract: Candida causes an estimated half-billion cases of vulvovaginal candidiasis (VVC) every year. VVC is most commonly caused by Candida albicans , which, in this setting, triggers nonprotective neutrophil infiltration, aggressive local inflammation, and symptomatic disease. Despite its prevalence, little is known about the molecular mechanisms underpinning the immunopathology of this fungal infection. In this study, we describe the molecular determinant of VVC immunopathology and a potentially straightforward way to prevent disease. In response to zinc limitation, C. albicans releases a trace mineral binding molecule called Pra1 (pH-regulated antigen). Here, we show that the PRA1 gene is strongly up-regulated during vaginal infections and that its expression positively correlated with proinflammatory cytokine concentrations in women. Genetic deletion of PRA1 prevented vaginal inflammation in mice, and application of a zinc solution down-regulated expression of the gene and also blocked immunopathology. We also show that treatment of women suffering from recurrent VVC with a zinc gel prevented reinfections. We have therefore identified a key mediator of symptomatic VVC, giving us an opportunity to develop a range of preventative measures for combatting this disease.

doi:10.1126/scitranslmed.ads0848.abstract: Cartilage lesions do not heal spontaneously and predispose to osteoarthritis. Functional cartilage tissues, engineered using autologous chondrocytes, have a therapeutic advantage over conventional cellular therapies in preclinical studies. Here, we tested whether ex vivo maturation of engineered grafts for cartilage repair leads to improved patient benefit. Using autologous nasal chondrocytes (NCs), we tested whether implantation of in vitro–matured NC-tissue-engineered cartilage (N-TEC) versus undifferentiated NC-cell-activated matrices (N-CAM) in focal cartilage lesions would result in a superior clinical outcome. The prospective, randomized, parallel, open-label phase-2 trial ( ClinicalTrials.gov , NCT02673905) enrolled 108 patients in five hospitals from four countries. Patients ranging in age from 30 to 46 years with full-thickness knee cartilage defects (size, 2.7 to 6.0 square centimeters) were equally randomized and treated with N-TEC or N-CAM. The primary preregistered outcome was the overall Knee Injury Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS) at 24 months. N-TEC, which underwent a longer NC culture time, was phenotypically, structurally, and functionally more like hyaline cartilage than N-CAM. The overall KOOS increased with clinical relevance in both groups compared with preoperative values. KOOS was higher at 24 months for N-TEC [85; interquartile range (IQR), 74 to 91] than for N-CAM (79; IQR, 65 to 85). N-TEC, but not N-CAM, was similarly effective in patients with larger defects or revision surgery. Radiologically, N-TEC resulted in a superior composition of both repair tissue and surrounding cartilage, whereas structural scores were similar. This trial validates the clinical efficacy of NC-based grafts for articular cartilage repair and supports the clinical relevance of engineering mature tissues, even for patients with more challenging cartilage defects.

doi:10.1126/scitranslmed.adv2106.abstract: Hepatocyte apoptosis is a key feature of metabolic dysfunction–associated steatohepatitis (MASH), but the fate of apoptotic hepatocytes in MASH is poorly understood. Here, we explore the hypotheses that clearance of dead hepatocytes by liver macrophages (efferocytosis) is impaired in MASH because of low expression of the efferocytosis receptor T cell immunoglobulin and mucin domain containing 4 (TIM4; gene Timd4 ) by MASH liver macrophages, which then drives liver fibrosis in MASH. We show that apoptotic hepatocytes accumulate in human and experimental MASH, using mice fed the fructose-palmitate-cholesterol (FPC) diet or the high-fat, choline-deficient amino acid–defined (HF-CDAA) diet. Apoptotic hepatocyte accumulation is associated with impaired efferocytosis and loss of TIM4. Administration of neutralizing anti-TIM4 antibodies or genetic deletion of Timd4 in Kupffer cells of FPC and HF-CDAA diet–fed mice decreased efferocytosis by liver macrophages, increased profibrotic activation of collagen-producing hepatic stellate cells (HSCs), and accelerated the progression to fibrotic MASH. Genetic restoration of macrophage Timd4 in FPC and HF-CDAA diet–fed MASH mice or cell therapy with TIM4 + macrophages enhanced apoptotic hepatocyte clearance and decreased HSC activation and liver fibrosis. Studies using an ex vivo macrophage HSC cross-talk model and the HF-CDAA MASH model revealed that inactivation of HSCs by efferocytosing macrophages involved macrophage reprogramming to secrete interleukin-10 (IL-10), which activated the IL-10 receptor on HSCs to dampen their profibrotic activation. These findings reveal a key process in the progression from hepatic steatosis to early MASH fibrosis and identify a mechanism-based therapeutic strategy to prevent fibrotic MASH progression.

doi:10.1126/scitranslmed.ady4852.abstract: The incidence and mortality of high-grade endometrial cancers are increasing, and heterozygous hotspot mutations in PPP2R1A are drivers of the most aggressive forms of uterine cancer. PPP2R1A encodes the Aα scaffolding subunit of the heterotrimeric phosphatase PP2A. These recurrent mutations, specifically at the Pro179 and Ser256 residues, disrupt the binding of tumor-suppressive substrate-directing B56 and B55 subunits to the PP2A scaffolding subunit while maintaining binding to other regulatory subunits. Here, we identified a series of molecular glues that correct PP2A trimer formation in the context of the P179R (Pro179→Arg) and S256F (Ser256→Phe) mutants. A small-molecule library was designed to fit into the pocket at the binding interface of the Aα/B56α/C heterotrimer. The lead molecule, RPT04402, promoted B56α heterotrimerization to the AαP179R and AαS256F mutant scaffolds. In mice, RPT04402 treatment drove tumor regressions and extended median survival in multiple independent mutant cell lines and patient-derived xenografts, proving a robust single-agent activity. This activity was abrogated upon knockout of B56α. Combined, these data demonstrate that PP2A molecular glues are a promising first-in-class therapy that might benefit patients with PPP2R1A mutant uterine cancer by targeting a driver of this aggressive disease.

doi:10.1126/scitranslmed.adz2015.abstract: Proliferative lupus nephritis (LN) is triggered by deposition of autoantibodies in glomeruli and paralleled by a T cell–rich kidney infiltrate. Although these T cells have been attributed to the propagation of tissue injury, it is unclear how they are activated and whether T cell autoreactivity drives local inflammation. Kidney-infiltrating T cells are also observed in urine, where they have high resemblance to interstitial T cells. Therefore, urinary T cells are a proxy for investigating tissue pathogenesis. Here, we analyzed urinary T cells to elucidate whether a kidney-specific T cell autoimmune reaction contributes to tubulointerstitial inflammation in LN. Using single-cell RNA sequencing, we compared transcriptomes and clonotypes of T cells from the blood and urine of patients with active LN and showed that urinary T cells were mostly activated CD8 effector memory cells recruited from a circulating CX3CR1 + subset. Several urinary CD8 T cell clones were expanded. However, upon in vitro testing of their T cell receptors, we did not observe autoreactivity against autologous tubular epithelial cells. Instead, ~20% of expanded clonotypes were Epstein-Barr virus–specific or cytomegalovirus-specific, but respective viral antigens were undetectable in kidney biopsies or urine. Conversely, kidney-infiltrating T cells had access to interleukin-15 and interferon-β (IFN-β), and stimulation with these cytokines was sufficient to trigger degranulation and production of tumor necrosis factor, IFN-γ, and granzyme K. Together, these results show that CD8 + CX3CR1 + T cells are recruited into the kidney in LN, where they are activated by cytokines, enabling them to contribute to local inflammation.

doi:10.1126/scitranslmed.adz4815.abstract: Aging is characterized by progressive functional decline, yet metabolomic signatures across the human life span remain incompletely defined. Here, we profiled plasma metabolomes from 18,476 participants aged 1 to 96 years across six centers in China using nano-assisted laser desorption/ionization mass spectrometry (LDI-MS) and identified 56 representative age-associated metabolites. In a healthy cohort, we developed a stacking ensemble model to estimate metabolomic age and quantified metabolomic age acceleration (mAA) as each individual's deviation from chronological age. Higher mAA was associated with health deterioration and unfavorable lifestyles. During follow-up from 2019 to 2025, individuals with accelerated mAA showed increased risk of incident chronic diseases, such as fatty liver disease, hypertension, and diabetes, as well as increased all-cause mortality. In a disease cohort, we further developed a mortality-linked metabolomic metric (age deviation) that quantified individualized departures from age-expected mortality risk inferred from plasma metabolites. Age deviation was associated with established composite health measures and increased with multisystem disease involvement and higher multimorbidity burden. Together, these findings support the potential of plasma metabolomic profiling as a scalable, life span-wide approach for deriving clinically interpretable metabolomic aging metrics associated with health status, chronic disease risk, and mortality.

doi:10.1126/scitranslmed.aea8738.abstract: Recent evidence implicates a metabolic switch in afferent spinal circuits as a key driver of the transition from acute pain– to chronic pain–related behaviors in mice after tissue injury, yet the cellular substrates and functional consequences remain incompletely defined. Using a combination of pharmacological and genetic approaches, we investigated whether metabolic reprogramming in spinal cord cell populations constitutes a causal mechanism linking peripheral injury to the progression to pain chronicity. After peripheral injury induced by a hindpaw formalin injection in mice, single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) revealed that spinal oligodendrocytes down-regulated transcripts for myelin protein synthesis and up-regulated transcripts important for lipid biosynthesis. Comparative lipidomics showed that this resource reallocation after peripheral injury was associated with disrupted spinal myelin composition. Moreover, axonal integrity was compromised, causing neuronal accumulation of amyloid precursor protein, enhanced β-site amyloid precursor protein–cleaving enzyme 1 (BACE1) expression, and increased insoluble amyloid-β 42 (Aβ 42 ) during a critical temporal window for the transition to pain chronicity. Blocking Aβ 42 production by BACE1 inhibition or clearing Aβ 42 by intrathecal 4G8 monoclonal antibody injection prevented the emergence of persistent pain after hindpaw formalin injection. Oligodendrocyte-specific deletion of N -acylethanolamine acid amidase, a key regulator of cell metabolism and pain, prevented Aβ 42 release and chronic pain development induced by formalin injection or sciatic nerve ligation. These findings uncover an unexpected mechanistic link between chronic pain and amyloid pathology and identify the NAAA→Aβ 42 pathway as a target for disease-modifying intervention.

doi:10.1126/scitranslmed.aec5740.abstract: Microglial dysfunction is increasingly implicated in Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathogenesis, with loss-of-function variants in the microglial receptor TREM2 as major risk factors for late-onset AD. We report VG-3927, an oral, CNS-penetrant small-molecule TREM2 agonist that engages the transmembrane domains of TREM2 and its adaptor DAP12 to promote higher-order receptor complex formation and downstream signaling. VG-3927 and tool compound VG-3909 exhibited (sub)nanomolar potency, cooperated with endogenous ligands including amyloid-β (Aβ), and restored signaling in disease-associated TREM2 variants. In human iPSC-derived neuron-microglia-astrocyte cultures, VG-3927 reduced inflammatory cytokines and markers of neuronal damage. In 5xFAD amyloidosis mice expressing the common variant of hTREM2 (5xFAD;hTREM2CV), VG-3909 induced neuroprotective transcriptional reprogramming of microglia, particularly in the plaque niche; enhanced Aβ phagocytosis; and boosted brain glucose metabolism. By contrast, a TREM2 agonist antibody, which may be sequestered by soluble TREM2 (sTREM2), failed to engage plaque microglia. In a first-in-human, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 1 trial (NCT06343636, n = 115), VG-3927 was well tolerated across single and multiple ascending doses of up to 140 milligrams. Pharmacokinetics supported once-daily dosing with high CNS penetration (CSF-to-unbound plasma ratio of 0.91). VG-3927 induced dose-dependent reductions in CSF sTREM2, a biomarker of target engagement, consistent across healthy and elderly participants and participants with AD, supporting further clinical development in AD under the new designation SAR448851.

doi:10.1126/scitranslmed.aec9689.abstract: The transition from acute kidney injury (AKI) to chronic kidney disease (CKD) remains a major clinical problem with unclear underlying mechanisms. Emerging evidence suggests that alterations in tryptophan metabolism, particularly in the production of downstream metabolites such as quinolinic acid (QA), play a role in renal pathophysiology. QA, an intermediate in de novo nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide biosynthesis, is metabolized by quinolinate phosphoribosyltransferase (QPRT). We investigated whether QA contributes to kidney injury using models of folic acid-induced AKI-to-CKD transition and cisplatin-induced AKI, genetic and exogenous approaches to alter QA, and clinical observations. Untargeted kidney metabolomics identified QA as one of the most elevated metabolites after folic acid injury. After folic acid injury, Qprt haploinsufficiency exacerbated kidney injury and fibrosis-related gene expression; aged Qprt-haploinsufficient mice exhibited increased fibrosis-associated gene expression without overt renal dysfunction. Exogenous QA administration increased serum creatinine in uninjured mice and worsened renal dysfunction and fibrosis-related gene expression in the folic acid AKI-to-CKD model. Conversely, mice deficient in either 3-hydroxyanthranilate 3,4-dioxygenase (HAAO) or kynurenine 3-monooxygenase (KMO), which reduce flux toward QA, showed improved renal outcomes after folic acid injury and cisplatin-induced AKI. Multimodal spatial metabolomics analysis of kidney biopsies from patients with AKI revealed QA accumulation in regions of inflammatory infiltration. Last, children with CKD exhibited higher urinary QA compared with healthy individuals. These findings underscore QA as a potential mediator of kidney injury and a therapeutic target for preventing the progression from AKI to CKD.

doi:10.1126/scitranslmed.aee4629.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) now enables the exploration of vast chemical and sequence spaces, the design of synthesizable antibiotics, and the prioritization of safe, mechanism-diverse candidates through integrated modeling and accelerated testing. Here, we survey recent advances in AI for both small-molecule and peptide antimicrobial drugs, highlight emerging data and reporting standards, and outline translational pathways and regulatory hurdles needed to bring these agents to patients.

doi:10.1126/scitranslmed.aef8416.abstract: Integrated strategies to combat antibiotic-resistant bacteria and fungi require innovative commercial models, new discovery platforms, standardized genomic surveillance, and streamlined clinical trials. Next-generation approaches should align societal impact with investment to ensure rapid global public health gains.

doi:10.1126/scitranslmed.aeh1292.abstract: The continuous antigenic evolution of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) has repeatedly undermined the effectiveness of monoclonal antibody (mAb) therapies, underscoring the need for innovative approaches that improve therapeutic mAb breadth and durability of protection. Here, we engineered messenger ribonucleic acid (mRNA)-encoded bispecific antibodies (bsAbs) that, upon intravenous administration in lipid nanoparticles, achieved high serum concentrations, extended half-life, and serum neutralizing titers exceeding 1:10,000 in human neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn)-expressing mice. To enhance resilience to viral escape, we used structure-guided computational design to introduce Fc modifications that promoted selective homodimerization, thereby enabling codelivery of multiple mRNA-encoded bsAbs with cognate heavy chain pairing. In vivo expression of a triple bsAb combination resulted in broad serum neutralization of historical and contemporary SARS-CoV-2 variants, including the highly mutated BA.3.2.2 lineage. Preexposure prophylaxis with the mRNA-delivered bsAb combination conferred protection against SARS-CoV-2 XBB.1.5 challenge, preventing weight loss and decreasing viral burden in the lungs compared with vehicle control treatment. Together, the results provide proof of principle for mRNA-based delivery of Fc-engineered bsAb combinations to combat SARS-CoV-2 and potentially other rapidly evolving pathogens.

doi:10.1126/scitranslmed.aei2870.abstract: Innate immune signaling through inflammasome activation has been implicated in the pathogenesis of multiple sclerosis (MS). We previously demonstrated that nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs), drugs approved to treat HIV and hepatitis B virus infections, and kamuvudines, safer NRTI derivatives, both inhibit inflammasome activation. Here, we report that in the experimental autoimmune encephalitis mouse model of MS, treatment with kamuvudine-9 (K-9), an NRTI derivative with an enhanced safety profile, prevented further neurological deficits and reversed preexisting paralysis and vision loss. K-9 promoted myelin and axonal preservation in the mouse spinal cord and abolished the increase in serum neurofilament light (NfL) chain. K-9 disrupted interactions between nucleotide-binding domain leucine-rich repeat (NLR) pyrin domain-containing protein 3 (NLRP3) and NIMA-related kinase 7 (NEK7) and between NLRP3 and NLR CARD domain containing 4 (NLRC4), inhibiting dual inflammasome activation. K-9 also exhibited appropriate safety and pharmacokinetic characteristics and biodistribution. In three distinct human cohorts, there was a lower incidence of MS in those individuals receiving NRTIs for HIV infection, preexposure prophylaxis for HIV, or hepatitis B virus infection. NRTI use was also associated with a reduction in relapse rate in individuals with MS. These findings provide a rationale for further investigating K-9 for treating MS.

doi:10.1158/0008-5472.can-25-2084.abstract: Growth-induced solid stress and fluid pressure contribute to tumor progression and drug resistance. Beyond tumor endogenous physical forces, cells in the tumor microenvironment may also experience external macroscopic mechanical stress, and some tumors preferentially develop in weight-bearing regions with higher focal pressure. Characterization of the impact of macroscopic mechanical stress on the tumor microenvironment could help uncover the mechanistic links between external mechanical forces and increased tumor incidence. Here, we showed that recurrent macroscopic mechanical stress disrupts nuclear envelope integrity, leading to spatial reorganization and fibroblast subtype changes at the tumor-stromal interface. In mouse models of plantar melanoma, exogenous mechanical stress induced nuclear envelope rupture in melanoma cells and increased LRRC15-positive myofibroblasts. Reduction of nuclear envelope integrity through inducible deletion of Lmna likewise increased LRRC15-positive myofibroblast generation. Co-culture with myofibroblasts promoted nuclear envelope rupture in melanoma cells in 3D culture, suggesting a positive feedback loop. In addition, mechanical stress-driven transcriptomic changes in tumor and stromal cells were observed alongside enhanced lymph node metastasis and immunotherapy resistance. Analysis of human melanoma samples revealed mechanical stress-associated stromal remodeling and a higher incidence of lymph node metastasis in tumors arising in mechanically stressed regions, although these features were not significantly associated with overall survival. Together, these findings suggest that macroscopic mechanical stress may influence cancer progression by inducing nuclear envelope damage and reshaping tumor-stromal interactions.

doi:10.1158/0008-5472.can-25-2748.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is a lethal malignancy 20% more likely to develop in Black African Americans (BAA) compared to Non-African Americans (NAA). Large-scale gene expression analysis of tumor subtypes and cellular microenvironments in a diverse PDAC cohort could help provide insights into cell and molecular differences in BAA cancer cells. Here, we conducted a multi-omics interrogation of BAA versus NAA PDAC using whole exome sequencing, spatial transcriptomics (ST), and spatial proteomics. Whole exome sequencing confirmed patient ancestry and showed no significant differences in driver mutations between race groups. BAA PDAC tumors had significantly fewer classical molecular subtype cells with no change in more aggressive basal-like cells. Instead, BAA patients showed a significant enrichment of the intermediate/hybrid subtype compared to NAA patients. BAA tumors also displayed increased B cell and reduced myeloid cell interactions compared to NAA tumors. Analysis of tertiary lymphoid structures in a validation cohort revealed that tumors in BAA patients displayed larger TLS size and number compared to NAA. In conclusion, these findings identify an increased intermediate molecular subtype signature in BAA tumors at the expense of cells with a classical subtype, accompanied by a distinct immune cell composition and spatial distribution. This study highlights that health disparities in patients of different ancestries may have a molecular basis that influences tumor aggressiveness and the immune response, which may inform therapeutic strategies.

doi:10.1158/0008-5472.can-25-4782.abstract: Abstract The Tn antigen, a truncated O-glycan, is frequently elevated in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). Multiple therapeutic approaches targeting Tn have been developed, but they have not demonstrated clear efficacy signals in early-phase clinical studies. Improving Tn-targeted strategies in PDAC will require both overcoming the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment and defining pathways by which truncated O-glycans promote growth and immune evasion. In this study, we show that Tn reshapes the tumor immune landscape of PDAC. Expression of Tn antigen on PDAC cells enhanced proliferation in vitro and tumor growth in vivo. Tn expression remodeled the immune microenvironment, skewing tumor-associated macrophages toward M2-like phenotypes, reducing cross-presenting dendritic cells, and expanding myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSC). Single-cell RNA sequencing confirmed the expansion of MDSCs and downregulation of antigen processing and presentation in the immune cell infiltrate of Tn+ tumors. Tumor-intrinsic transcriptomic analyses revealed the activation of TNFα/NF-κB signaling and induction of IL34, a cytokine linked to monocyte survival and differentiation in Tn antigen–expressing tumors. Additionally, high Tn expression in both organoids derived from patients with pancreatic cancer and in PDAC mouse models was associated with increased IL34 expression. The genetic deletion of Il34 in PDAC cells attenuated Tn-driven tumorigenesis and reduced MDSC infiltration, whereas recombinant IL34 promoted myeloid cell differentiation and proliferation in vitro. Together, these findings establish a glyco–immune–cytokine axis in which truncated O-glycans contribute to IL34-mediated immunosuppression, providing mechanistic insights and potential therapeutic targets in PDAC. Significance: Altered glycosylation stimulates TNF-α/NF-κB signaling and induces IL-34-mediated accumulation of suppressive myeloid cells in pancreatic cancer, providing a myeloid-mediated mechanism of immunosuppression that could guide the development of therapies targeting glycosylation.

doi:10.1158/0008-5472.can-25-5347.abstract: Lung squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC) is an aggressive subtype of non-small cell lung cancer with limited targeted therapeutic options and incompletely defined immune-regulatory dependencies. Here, we identified atypical chemokine receptor 3 (ACKR3) as a squamous-enriched regulator that restrains malignant progression in LUSC. Integrative analyses of human LUSC datasets, autochthonous genetically engineered mouse models, and ex vivo organoid systems showed that ACKR3 loss accelerated tumor growth and remodeled the immune microenvironment, marked by reduced CD8⁺ T cell infiltration and increased T cell exhaustion. Mechanistically, ACKR3 limited activation of the MIF-CD74-PD-L1 axis, thereby constraining tumor-cell PD-L1 expression and preserving antitumor immune surveillance. In preclinical LUSC models, treatment with the ACKR3-directed PD-L1 degrader KineTAC, a bispecific molecule that co-engages ACKR3 and PD-L1 to promote lysosomal degradation of PD-L1, enhanced antitumor efficacy, particularly in combination with chemotherapy. Together, these findings define ACKR3 as a squamous-associated immune checkpoint regulator and nominate ACKR3-directed PD-L1 degradation as a tumor-selective therapeutic strategy for LUSC.

doi:10.1158/0008-5472.can-25-5766.abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most common and deadly primary brain tumor in adults, characterized by diffuse infiltrative lesions, distinct oncogenic alterations, and a suppressive tumor immune microenvironment (TIME). These traits, however, are not fully recapitulated in current syngeneic murine glioma models, thereby limiting the pre-clinical development of novel therapies. Here we developed murine GBM models with patient-specific mutations that shared striking resemblance with human disease. Mosaic analysis with dual-recombinase mediated cassette exchange (MADR) and CRISPR-Cas9 were leveraged to generate autochthonous tumor models with single-copy somatic transgenesis of murine epidermal growth factor receptor variant III (mEGFRvIII) and loss-of-function mutations commonly observed in GBM. Characterization of a model lacking Pten and Cdkn2a (mEGFRvIII-PC) via histopathologic analyses, functional assays, and single-cell RNA sequencing showed these tumors developed as diffuse, infiltrative lesions with ill-defined margins and a necrotic core. The TIME was primarily comprised of microglia with minimal lymphocyte infiltration, recapitulating patient tumors. Furthermore, these tumors displayed intrinsic resistance to immune checkpoint blockade, potentially due to poor myeloid cell antigen presentation and T cell priming. Additionally, mEGFRvIII-PC cells were the most resistant to antigen-specific T cell-induced cytotoxicity and simultaneously promoted T cell exhaustion, while murine interferon-γ (mIFN-γ) stimulation induced a greater response in vitro with enhanced upregulation of PD-L1 relative to MHC-I. In sum, these findings demonstrate the improved fidelity of the mEGFRvIII-PC model to patient tumors and support its use in developing and refining novel therapeutic paradigms for GBM.

doi:10.1158/0008-5472.can-25-5866.abstract: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) is characterized by profound metabolic reprogramming and substantial inherited susceptibility. The molecular mechanisms linking germline risk variation to tumor metabolic reprogramming could potentially be exploited for precision interventions. Here, we aimed to delineate the germline regulatory architecture underlying ccRCC susceptibility and to determine how inherited noncoding variation influences mitochondrial metabolism and tumor progression. Whole-genome sequencing and transcriptomic profiling of matched ccRCC tumor and adjacent normal kidney tissues were integrated with cross-ancestry genome-wide association, cis-expression quantitative trait locus, transcriptome-wide association, and fine-mapping analyses. LINC02068 was identified as a genetically regulated tumor suppressor associated with inherited ccRCC susceptibility, and cross-ancestry fine-mapping prioritized rs234043 as a candidate causal variant. The rs234043 risk allele preferentially recruited HOXC8 and repressed LINC02068 transcription. Reduced LINC02068 expression promoted malignant cellular phenotypes and was associated with adverse clinical outcomes. Mechanistically, LINC02068 localized to mitochondria, interacted with the co-chaperone DNAJA3, and promoted DNAJA3 destabilization, thereby attenuating mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation. Allele-specific editing and genetic rescue experiments further supported a functional rs234043-HOXC8-LINC02068-DNAJA3 regulatory axis driving ccRCC progression. Pharmacologic impairment of mitochondrial complex I suppressed ccRCC cell migration and proliferation. These findings establish a mechanistic link between a germline noncoding variation and mitochondrial metabolic reprogramming in ccRCC and identify targeting oxidative phosphorylation as a potential avenue for precision therapy.

doi:10.1158/0008-5472.can-26-0507.abstract: Epigenetic dysregulation plays a vital role in the progression of endometrial cancer (EC), yet targeted treatment options remain limited. Here, we identified the histone acetyltransferase KAT5 as a therapeutic target in EC. KAT5 was significantly overexpressed in EC and correlated with poor patient outcome. Silencing KAT5 inhibited EC cell proliferation and tumor growth. KAT5-deficient EC cells exhibited impaired cytoskeletal dynamics, leading to heightened DNA damage and increased micronuclei formation. The release of micronuclear DNA into the cytoplasm activated the cGAS-STING pathway, thereby amplifying proinflammatory immune responses. Mechanistically, KAT5 acetylated H2A.Z to transcriptionally activate Arp2/3 complex genes, promoting actin polymerization and chromosomal stability. Inhibition of Arp2/3 or depletion of its subunit ARPC5 replicated the effects of KAT5 loss, whereas restoring ARPC5 mitigated chromosomal instability and cGAS activation. In transplantation models of EC cell lines and syngeneic murine Trp53-/-;Pten-/- EC organoids, pharmacological inhibition of KAT5 with NU9056 suppressed tumor progression and enhanced immune cell infiltration. NU9056 also induced Arp2/3 disruption, genomic instability, and cGAS-STING activation in patient-derived organoids from clinical endometrial cancer samples. Together, these findings highlight KAT5 as a promising therapeutic target in EC that influences chromatin remodeling, cytoskeletal dynamics, and immune modulation.

doi:10.1158/0008-5472.can-26-0860.abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) driven by gain-of-function mutations in CTNNB1 (CTNNB1GOF) that stabilize β-catenin exhibits a profoundly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME), rendering it resistant to immune checkpoint blockade (ICB). Metabolic reprogramming is increasingly recognized as a crucial mediator of immune activity, highlighting the need to elucidate the specific metabolic mechanisms underlying immune exclusion in CTNNB1GOF HCC. Here, we identified a critical metabolic-immune network orchestrated by co-mutations of CTNNB1 and ARID2. Integrative analysis of HCC patient cohorts and a de novo MYC/CTNNB1GOF HCC mouse model revealed that tumors harboring concurrent CTNNB1 and ARID2 mutations exhibited a more immune-active TME and improved survival compared to tumors with CTNNB1 mutations alone. Mechanistically, β-catenin and ARID2 cooperatively enhanced the transcription of tryptophan 2,3-dioxygenase (TDO2), leading to accelerated kynurenine production and activation of the aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) in myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs). This metabolic axis established an immunosuppressive milieu characterized by MDSC accumulation and impaired T cell function. Genetic ablation of Arid2 in CTNNB1GOF HCC attenuated TDO2-dependent kynurenine synthesis, reduced MDSC infiltration, and enhanced CD8⁺ T cell cytotoxicity, thereby sensitizing tumors to anti-PD-1 therapy. Clinically, co-mutations of CTNNB1 and ARID2 correlated with elevated immune infiltration and favorable ICB responses across multiple human cancers, including HCC. Importantly, pharmacological inhibition of AhR phenocopied the immunomodulatory effect of ARID2 loss and, when combined with anti-PD-1, robustly reversed the immune-cold phenotype of CTNNB1GOF HCC. These findings reveal TDO2-kynurenine-AhR signaling as a pivotal metabolic pathway enforcing immune evasion in CTNNB1-mutant HCC.

doi:10.1158/0008-5472.can-26-2050.abstract: The RAS/MAPK pathway is among the most frequently dysregulated in human cancer, predominantly driven by activating mutations across RAS and BRAF in a broad spectrum of tumor types. The recent clinical validation of direct inhibitors of RAS, long considered undruggable, has reenergized the field and renewed focus on targeting the full RAS/MAPK axis. MEK, a central node in MAPK signaling, remains an attractive mutation-agnostic target, yet the efficacy of first-generation MEK inhibitors has been limited by pathway reactivation in tumors and by on-target, off-tissue toxicity. In this issue of Cancer Research, Kolitz and colleagues describe atebimetinib, a novel MEK inhibitor that also prevents feedback-induced MEK phosphorylation by RAF. The uniquely short plasma half-life of atebimetinib enables deep cyclic inhibition (DCI): transient but profound MEK/ERK output suppression with full recovery between doses. At each drug's tolerability limit, atebimetinib outperformed the MEK inhibitor binimetinib across multiple RAS- and BRAF-mutant tumor models. Whether DCI or suppression of MEK phosphorylation is the primary driver of the improved therapeutic window and how atebimetinib compares with the clinical standard and other MEK-targeting agents remain important open questions, but the work makes a compelling case that novel pharmacology can unlock therapeutic spaces at targets long considered exhausted. See related article by Kolitz et al., p. 5223.

doi:10.1158/0008-5472.can-26-4373.abstract: The exquisite antigen specificity of T cells is one foundation of modern cancer immunotherapy. The therapeutic efficacy of checkpoint blockade, cancer vaccines, and engineered T-cell therapies, all appear to depend on T cells capable of recognizing specific antigens displayed by tumor cells. In a recent issue of Nature Immunology, Smith and colleagues challenge this paradigm by demonstrating that local activation of virus-specific memory T cells can eliminate tumors without direct tumor-cell recognition. Instead, activated T cells initiate a multicellular inflammatory response involving IFNγ, TNF, nitric oxide and recruited myeloid cells that collectively induce tumor-cell death. These findings separate the antigen specificity required for T-cell activation from that required for tumor killing and expand the role of T cells from direct cytotoxic effectors to organizers of a broader antitumor response. Together, these findings broaden the potential scope of T-cell-mediated antitumor immunity beyond the constraints of direct tumor-antigen recognition.

doi:10.1158/0008-5472.can-26-4375.abstract: Targeted drug conjugates often rely on receptor-mediated internalization and intracellular trafficking for payload release. This requirement limits the range of tumor-associated targets that can be effectively exploited and has motivated the development of strategies for extracellular drug release. Wen and colleagues introduce a binding-to-release (BTR) strategy in which target engagement itself serves as the trigger for payload release. The authors used ligand-directed chemistry to develop phosphorus(V)-phenol exchange (PhoPEx) chemistry that exploits proximity between an electrophilic linker and a nucleophilic tyrosine residue within the binding pocket of the target to initiate target-triggered payload release. Through optimization of the phenol-based scaffold, the authors evaluated 15 PhoPEx compounds to balance hydrolytic stability and reaction kinetics. The authors then used fibroblast activation protein, a poorly internalizing stromal target, to test the BTR strategy using a membrane-permeable payload, resulting in improved tumor drug exposure and antitumor activity in preclinical models. The BTR strategy was further extended to imaging applications and other targets, including programmed death-ligand 1. Although demonstrated primarily with small-molecule conjugates, BTR introduces an alternative approach for targeted drug delivery of poorly internalizing targets in which target binding could be exploited as a trigger, potentially expanding the landscape of tumor-associated targets accessible to targeted therapeutics.

doi:10.1158/1078-0432.ccr-26-2916.abstract: Abstract REMATCH, a single-institution phase II study, evaluated reduced-volume surgery in patients with locally advanced head and neck cancer responding to neoadjuvant immunochemotherapy. Two-year disease-free survival was 90%, with universal laryngeal preservation. The trial advances organ preservation by reducing the extent and intensity of local therapy rather than substituting modalities.

doi:10.1158/1940-6207.capr-26-0170.abstract: Abstract The metabolic reprogramming taking place during early lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) progression remain poorly understood. While early-stage LUAD frequently demonstrates low 18F-2-fluorodeoxyglucose (18FDG) uptake on positron emission tomography (PET), it is unclear whether this reflects metabolic quiescence or alternative glucose utilization pathways. We hypothesized that early lesions are metabolically active but preferentially utilize sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2), a non-canonical glucose transporter with low 18FDG affinity. This study investigates metabolic activity in early-stage LUAD and glucose transporter expression patterns across the adenocarcinoma spectrum. LDH, SGLT2 and GLUT1 expression were evaluated by immunohistochemistry in human lung cancers and compared with normal lung and benign inflammation. Expression levels were correlated with structural and radiologic features including tumor size, invasion, histology, radiographic features and PET avidity. Glycolysis was elevated in premalignant and early LUAD as indicated by LDH expression. SGLT2 was highly expressed in preinvasive and minimally invasive LUAD compared to normal lung and invasive tumors. Conversely, GLUT1 was upregulated in invasive, high-grade tumors. Radiographically, SGLT2 expression was associated with subsolid nodules and low PET avidity, while GLUT1 expression was higher in nodules with a solid component and high 18FDG avidity. Notably, SGLT2 was not elevated in inflammatory lesions compared to normal lung, unlike GLUT1, which was frequently upregulated in inflammation. Early lung adenocarcinoma lesions exhibit aerobic glycolysis despite low FDG avidity and preferentially utilize SGLT2-mediated glucose uptake. These findings highlight a distinct metabolic profile in early LUAD and underscore the need for alternative imaging modalities to enhance the detection of early lesions.

doi:10.1158/2159-8290.cd-12-0263.abstract: Abstract Laboratory research and pharmacoepidemiology are providing converging evidence that the widely used antidiabetic drug metformin has antineoplastic activity, but there are caveats. Although population studies suggest that metformin exposure is associated with reduced cancer risk and/or improved prognosis, these data are mostly retrospective and nonrandomized. Laboratory models show antineoplastic activity, but metformin concentrations used in many experiments exceed those achieved with conventional doses used for diabetes treatment. Ongoing translational research should be useful in guiding design of clinical trials, not only to evaluate metformin at conventional antidiabetic doses, where reduction of elevated insulin levels may contribute to antineoplastic activity for certain subsets of patients, but also to explore more aggressive dosing of biguanides, which may lead to reprogramming of energy metabolism in a manner that could provide important opportunities for synthetic lethality through rational drug combinations or in the context of genetic lesions associated with hypersensitivity to energetic stress. Significance: There are tantalizing clues that justify the investigation of antineoplastic activities of biguanides. The complexity of their biologic effects requires further translational research to guide clinical trial design. Cancer Discov; 2(9); 778–90. ©2012 AACR.

doi:10.1158/2159-8290.cd-12-0429.abstract: Abstract RNA interference (RNAi) is a potent and specific mechanism for regulating gene expression. Harnessing RNAi to silence genes involved in disease holds promise for the development of a new class of therapeutics. Delivery is key to realizing the potential of RNAi, and lipid nanoparticles (LNP) have proved effective in delivery of siRNAs to the liver and to tumors in animals. To examine the activity and safety of LNP-formulated siRNAs in humans, we initiated a trial of ALN-VSP, an LNP formulation of siRNAs targeting VEGF and kinesin spindle protein (KSP), in patients with cancer. Here, we show detection of drug in tumor biopsies, siRNA-mediated mRNA cleavage in the liver, pharmacodynamics suggestive of target downregulation, and antitumor activity, including complete regression of liver metastases in endometrial cancer. In addition, we show that biweekly intravenous administration of ALN-VSP was safe and well tolerated. These data provide proof-of-concept for RNAi therapeutics in humans and form the basis for further development in cancer. Significance: The findings in this report show safety, pharmacokinetics, RNAi mechanism of action, and clinical activity with a novel first-in-class LNP-formulated RNAi therapeutic in patients with cancer. The ability to harness RNAi to facilitate specific multitargeting, as well as increase the number of druggable targets, has important implications for future drug development in oncology. Cancer Discov; 3(4); 406–17. ©2012 AACR. This article is highlighted in the In This Issue feature, p. 363

doi:10.1158/2159-8290.cd-13-0136.abstract: Abstract The tumor suppressor p53 is lost or mutated in about half of all human cancers, and in those tumors in which it is wild-type, mechanisms exist to prevent its activation. p53 loss not only prevents incipient tumor cells from undergoing oncogene-induced senescence and apoptosis, but also perturbs cell-cycle checkpoints. This enables p53-deficient tumor cells with DNA damage to continue cycling, creating a permissive environment for the acquisition of additional mutations. Theoretically, this could contribute to the evolution of a cancer genome that is conducive to metastasis. Importantly, p53 loss also results in the disruption of pathways that inhibit metastasis, and transcriptionally defective TP53 mutants are known to gain additional functions that promote metastasis. Here, we review the evidence supporting a role for p53 loss or mutation in tumor metastasis, with an emphasis on breast cancer. Significance: The metastatic potential of tumor cells can be positively influenced by loss of p53 or expression of p53 gain-of-function mutants. Understanding the mechanisms by which p53 loss and mutation promote tumor metastasis is crucial to understanding the biology of tumor progression and how to appropriately apply targeted therapies. Cancer Discov; 4(4); 405–14. ©2014 AACR.

doi:10.1158/2159-8290.cd-15-0283.abstract: Abstract T cell–mediated immunotherapies are promising cancer treatments. However, most patients still fail to respond to these therapies. The molecular determinants of immune resistance are poorly understood. We show that loss of PTEN in tumor cells in preclinical models of melanoma inhibits T cell–mediated tumor killing and decreases T-cell trafficking into tumors. In patients, PTEN loss correlates with decreased T-cell infiltration at tumor sites, reduced likelihood of successful T-cell expansion from resected tumors, and inferior outcomes with PD-1 inhibitor therapy. PTEN loss in tumor cells increased the expression of immunosuppressive cytokines, resulting in decreased T-cell infiltration in tumors, and inhibited autophagy, which decreased T cell–mediated cell death. Treatment with a selective PI3Kβ inhibitor improved the efficacy of both anti–PD-1 and anti–CTLA-4 antibodies in murine models. Together, these findings demonstrate that PTEN loss promotes immune resistance and support the rationale to explore combinations of immunotherapies and PI3K–AKT pathway inhibitors. Significance: This study adds to the growing evidence that oncogenic pathways in tumors can promote resistance to the antitumor immune response. As PTEN loss and PI3K–AKT pathway activation occur in multiple tumor types, the results support the rationale to further evaluate combinatorial strategies targeting the PI3K–AKT pathway to increase the efficacy of immunotherapy. Cancer Discov; 6(2); 202–16. ©2015 AACR. See related commentary by Rizvi and Chan, p. 128. This article is highlighted in the In This Issue feature, p. 109

doi:10.1158/2159-8290.cd-15-1177.abstract: Abstract It remains unclear how obesity worsens treatment outcomes in patients with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). In normal pancreas, obesity promotes inflammation and fibrosis. We found in mouse models of PDAC that obesity also promotes desmoplasia associated with accelerated tumor growth and impaired delivery/efficacy of chemotherapeutics through reduced perfusion. Genetic and pharmacologic inhibition of angiotensin-II type-1 receptor reverses obesity-augmented desmoplasia and tumor growth and improves response to chemotherapy. Augmented activation of pancreatic stellate cells (PSC) in obesity is induced by tumor-associated neutrophils (TAN) recruited by adipocyte-secreted IL1β. PSCs further secrete IL1β, and inactivation of PSCs reduces IL1β expression and TAN recruitment. Furthermore, depletion of TANs, IL1β inhibition, or inactivation of PSCs prevents obesity-accelerated tumor growth. In patients with pancreatic cancer, we confirmed that obesity is associated with increased desmoplasia and reduced response to chemotherapy. We conclude that cross-talk between adipocytes, TANs, and PSCs exacerbates desmoplasia and promotes tumor progression in obesity. Significance: Considering the current obesity pandemic, unraveling the mechanisms underlying obesity-induced cancer progression is an urgent need. We found that the aggravation of desmoplasia is a key mechanism of obesity-promoted PDAC progression. Importantly, we discovered that clinically available antifibrotic/inflammatory agents can improve the treatment response of PDAC in obese hosts. Cancer Discov; 6(8); 852–69. ©2016 AACR. See related commentary by Bronte and Tortora, p. 821. This article is highlighted in the In This Issue feature, p. 803

doi:10.1158/2159-8290.cd-17-1124.abstract: Abstract Regulatory T cells (Treg) are critical for maintaining self-tolerance and immune homeostasis, but their suppressive function can impede effective antitumor immune responses. FOXP3 is a transcription factor expressed in Tregs that is required for their function. However, the pathways and microenvironmental cues governing FOXP3 expression and Treg function are not completely understood. Herein, we report that YAP, a coactivator of the Hippo pathway, is highly expressed in Tregs and bolsters FOXP3 expression and Treg function in vitro and in vivo. This potentiation stemmed from YAP-dependent upregulation of activin signaling, which amplifies TGFβ/SMAD activation in Tregs. YAP deficiency resulted in dysfunctional Tregs unable to suppress antitumor immunity or promote tumor growth in mice. Chemical YAP antagonism and knockout or blockade of the YAP-regulated activin receptor similarly improved antitumor immunity. Thus, we identify YAP as an unexpected amplifier of a Treg-reinforcing pathway with significant potential as an anticancer immunotherapeutic target. Significance: Tregs suppress antitumor immunity, and pathways supporting their function can be novel immunotherapy targets. Here, the selective expression of YAP by Tregs, its importance for their function, and its unexpected enhancement of pro-Treg Activin/SMAD signaling are reported, as are validations of potential cancer-fighting antagonists of YAP and its regulatory targets. Cancer Discov; 8(8); 1026–43. ©2018 AACR. This article is highlighted in the In This Issue feature, p. 899

doi:10.1158/2159-8290.cd-18-0046.abstract: Abstract In many solid tumors, parasympathetic input is provided by the vagus nerve, which has been shown to modulate tumor growth. However, whether cholinergic signaling directly regulates progression of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) has not been defined. Here, we found that subdiaphragmatic vagotomy in LSL-Kras+/G12D;Pdx1-Cre (KC) mice accelerated PDAC development, whereas treatment with the systemic muscarinic agonist bethanechol restored the normal KC phenotype, thereby suppressing the accelerated tumorigenesis caused by vagotomy. In LSL-Kras+/G12D;LSL-Trp53+/R172H;Pdx1-Cre mice with established PDAC, bethanechol significantly extended survival. These effects were mediated in part through CHRM1, which inhibited downstream MAPK/EGFR and PI3K/AKT pathways in PDAC cells. Enhanced cholinergic signaling led to a suppression of the cancer stem cell (CSC) compartment, CD11b+ myeloid cells, TNFα levels, and metastatic growth in the liver. Therefore, these data suggest that cholinergic signaling directly and indirectly suppresses growth of PDAC cells, and therapies that stimulate muscarinic receptors may be useful in the treatment of PDAC. Significance: Subdiaphragmatic vagotomy or Chrm1 knockout accelerates pancreatic tumorigenesis, in part via expansion of the CSC compartment. Systemic administration of a muscarinic agonist suppresses tumorigenesis through MAPK and PI3K/AKT signaling, in early stages of tumor growth and in more advanced, metastatic disease. Therefore, CHRM1 may represent a potentially attractive therapeutic target. Cancer Discov; 8(11); 1458–73. ©2018 AACR. This article is highlighted in the In This Issue feature, p. 1333

doi:10.1158/2159-8290.cd-18-0710.abstract: Abstract Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is poorly responsive to therapies and histologically contains a paucity of neoplastic cells embedded within a dense desmoplastic stroma. Within the stroma, cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAF) secrete tropic factors and extracellular matrix components, and have been implicated in PDAC progression and chemotherapy resistance. We recently identified two distinct CAF subtypes characterized by either myofibroblastic or inflammatory phenotypes; however, the mechanisms underlying their diversity and their roles in PDAC remain unknown. Here, we use organoid and mouse models to identify TGFβ and IL1 as tumor-secreted ligands that promote CAF heterogeneity. We show that IL1 induces LIF expression and downstream JAK/STAT activation to generate inflammatory CAFs and demonstrate that TGFβ antagonizes this process by downregulating IL1R1 expression and promoting differentiation into myofibroblasts. Our results provide a mechanism through which distinct fibroblast niches are established in the PDAC microenvironment and illuminate strategies to selectively target CAFs that support tumor growth. Significance: Understanding the mechanisms that determine CAF heterogeneity in PDAC is a prerequisite for the rational development of approaches that selectively target tumor-promoting CAFs. Here, we identify an IL1-induced signaling cascade that leads to JAK/STAT activation and promotes an inflammatory CAF state, suggesting multiple strategies to target these cells in vivo. See related commentary by Ling and Chiao, p. 173. This article is highlighted in the In This Issue feature, p. 151
