doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1935087.abstract: Breast cancer is one of the most commonly diagnosed malignancies among women worldwide and is frequently curable when identified at an early stage. However, advanced and metastatic disease continue to account for a substantial proportion of breast cancer-related deaths, particularly among patients with aggressive subtypes such as inflammatory breast cancer (IBC), a clinicopathologic entity that spans hormone receptor-positive, HER2-positive, and triple-negative disease. Although advances in molecular profiling and systemic therapies have improved outcomes, substantial challenges persist in identifying patients at risk for recurrence, accurately assessing treatment response, and determining optimal therapeutic strategies. These challenges are driven by marked tumor heterogeneity and the dynamic interplay between malignant cells and their surrounding tumor microenvironment (TME). This review examines key barriers to the diagnosis and management of IBC, set against the broader landscape of advanced breast cancer. It discusses the clinical significance of late metastatic relapse, rapidly progressive disease, shortcomings of current prognostic frameworks, and the difficulties associated with monitoring metastatic involvement. Also highlighted are emerging approaches, including circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and other liquid biopsy technologies, that may enhance risk stratification, longitudinal surveillance, and detection of molecular resistance; these applications remain investigational, and established clinical approaches are distinguished from emerging strategies throughout. The TME is further explored as a critical determinant of tumor behavior, with emphasis on lymphoid and myeloid immune cells, stromal components, and immune checkpoint pathways that promote immune evasion and therapeutic resistance. Finally, this review surveys evolving treatment paradigms, including immunotherapeutic approaches, RNA-based diagnostics and therapeutics, most of which remain preclinical, and antibody-drug conjugates, which are expanding the therapeutic landscape for advanced disease. Together, these developments underscore the potential of integrating molecular, immunologic, and circulating biomarker data to enable more precise disease characterization and treatment selection, as essential for developing more effective, personalized strategies for patients with IBC and other advanced breast cancers.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1935795.abstract: Altered N-glycosylation plays a critical role in immune regulation, yet the spatial distribution of N-glycans within immune niches of immunologically "cold" tumors remain poorly defined. Here, we combine matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization mass spectrometry imaging (MALDI-MSI) with highly multiplexed immunohistochemistry using photocleavable mass tags. This integrated workflow enables spatial mapping of N-glycosylation and immune markers within lymphoid aggregates (LAs) in prostate and pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma tissues, two malignancies that respond poorly to immunotherapy. Given the role of N-glycosylation in immune regulation, spatially resolved N-glycan profiling may provide insight into molecular heterogeneity within lymphoid aggregates and their surrounding tumor microenvironment. To assess the relationship between N_glycosylation and immune markers, candidate LAs from tissue samples collected from patients with varying stages of prostate cancer, PCa (n=49) and pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, PDAC (n=26) were identified via histological stains prior to enzymatic release of N-glycans and MALDI-MSI. MALDI-IHC was used to target immune cell markers and extracellular matrix proteins. In tissues with LAs, three N-glycan structural classes were identified when detectable: oligo-mannose, fucosylated tetra-antennary, and bisecting N-acetylglucosamine in fucosylated bi,- tri- and tetra- antennary structures, with some N-glycans common to both tumor types. LAs showed predominantly central CD20 and CD44 signal surrounded by CD3 signal localized along the tumor periphery. Our analysis revealed unique N-glycan patterns within and surrounding LAs, with variable profiles in distant regions, highlighting heterogeneity in LA-associated N-glycan profiles.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1936986.abstract: Synchronous bilateral primary breast cancer (sBPBC) accounts for 2.9%-3.9% of newly diagnosed breast cancers, while cases with discordant histologic subtypes are exceptionally rare. We report on a 59-year-old woman with synchronous left-sided invasive ductal carcinoma (IDC) and right-sided invasive lobular carcinoma (ILC). The patient underwent bilateral breast-conserving surgery with sentinel lymph node biopsy, followed by adjuvant radiotherapy and endocrine therapy. No recurrence or metastasis was observed during the 12-month follow-up. To place the present case in the context of the existing literature, we comparatively reviewed seven previously reported cases of synchronous bilateral IDC and ILC. The comparison illustrated considerable heterogeneity in the clinicopathological characteristics, molecular profiles, nodal involvement, treatment strategies, and clinical outcomes. These findings support independent characterization of each breast lesion and individualized treatment planning based on the features of both tumors.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1937448.abstract: This study aimed to develop and validate an interpretable machine learning framework that combines semi-automated segmentation, intratumoral habitats derived from multiparametric MRI (mpMRI), and multiscale peritumoral radiomics to predict high-grade prostate cancer (HGPCa) before surgery. This retrospective dual-center study involved 274 patients, comprising 208 from Center 1 for development and 66 from Center 2 for external test. The clinical and imaging variables included patient age, serum PSA, fPSA, PSAD, maximum tumor diameter, PI-RADS scores, and anatomical zone distribution (PZ vs. TZ). The development cohort was randomly divided into a training cohort (n = 145) and an internal validation cohort (n = 63). Intratumoral habitats were delineated using semi-automated segmentation and unsupervised K-means clustering, while peritumoral radiomic features were extracted from concentric 1-, 3-, and 5-mm shells. Predictive classifiers were optimized through machine learning algorithms, particularly a multilayer perceptron (MLP) for the habitat signature. A combined clinical-radiomics nomogram was constructed, with SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) employed to enhance model interpretability. Subgroup analyses were performed to assess the discriminative performance of the combined nomogram across the peripheral zone (PZ) and transition zone (TZ). The combined nomogram exhibited superior diagnostic performance, achieving AUCs of 0.914, 0.903, and 0.797 in the training cohort, internal validation cohort, and external test cohort, respectively. The MLP-based habitat model showed good discriminative performance, with AUCs of 0.896, 0.897, and 0.782 across the training cohort, internal validation cohort, and external test cohort, respectively. Among the peritumoral regions, the 5-mm shell demonstrated the best discriminative performance. SHAP analysis identified Habitat 1 Shape Sphericity as the most influential feature. Subgroup analysis demonstrated the discriminatory ability of the combined nomogram in both the PZ (AUC: 0.796) and TZ (AUC: 0.753) subgroups. The integration of semi-automated segmentation-based habitat analysis and peritumoral radiomics provides a promising approach for preoperative risk stratification of prostate cancer.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1938611.abstract: Glioblastoma CNS WHO Grade 4 (GBM) is associated with poor prognosis and high recurrence rates despite the current therapeutic approaches. Conventional imaging, in particular Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI), is primarily used during follow-up to detect tumor recurrence but has limited ability to distinguish recurrence from therapy-related changes, such as tissue necrosis and postoperative scar tissue. Liquid biopsy using circulating tumor-specific serological biomarkers, such as miRNAs, provides a gene expression signature for early identification of GBM recurrence. This pilot "proof-of-concept" study investigated the potential of circulating tumor-derived miRNA in whole blood samples for early detection of tumor recurrence. In a previous whole-transcriptome screening (NGS) study, whole-blood samples (n = 33) from seven patients and tumor biopsies (n = 4) were used to identify biomarkers. Corresponding to tumor surgery and recurrence, miRNA expression was examined in pre-surgical blood samples and tumor tissues. In whole blood, we investigated whether a pattern could be identified indicating post-surgery downregulation, consistent with reduced tumor burden, followed by a return to pre-surgery levels at recurrence. We identified 1-19 miRNA species per patient (a total of 72 miRNAs) showing this pattern. In this manuscript, we present the qRT-PCR validation results. The 45 most promising miRNAs identified by NGS study were selected and quantified using qRT-PCR. In addition, miR-21 was included as a promising candidate reported in the literature. To address challenges in miRNA normalization, five normalization strategies and unnormalized raw Ct values were compared. Two normalization approaches (median DCt normalization and unnormalized raw Ct values) showed no systematic bias. Depending on the normalization method, the agreement between NGS and qRT-PCR ranged from 23.6 to 27.9%. Although the concordance between NGS and qRT-PCR was low at the individual-patient level, qRT-PCR identified a common set of 24 miRNAs differentially regulated across patients. Notably, miR-424-3p and miR-362-5p were shared by five of seven patients, followed by miR-1307-3p and miR-22-5p, each shared by four patients. Interestingly, miR-21 did not show the predefined recurrence-associated pattern in any patient. Blood-based miRNA profiling may complement imaging in longitudinal monitoring of GBM patients, although clinical benefits have not been confirmed, and validation in a larger independent cohort is required.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1939329.abstract: Acute leukemias require rapid subtype identification to guide timely treatment. Differentiation of acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), acute monocytic leukemia (AMoL/M5), and acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL/M3) often relies on specialized tests that may not be immediately available. This study evaluated differentiation only among patients already confirmed to have one of these three diagnoses, rather than screening an unselected population with suspected acute leukemia. This multicenter retrospective study included 9,398 newly diagnosed, previously untreated patients with established APL/M3, AMoL/M5, or ALL between May 2019 and May 2025 at four tertiary hospitals in China. Relapse, remission, follow-up, and non-initial disease episodes were excluded. Twenty-four routine hematological parameters were evaluated. One center served as the development cohort with five-fold stratified cross-validation, while three independent centers were reserved for external validation. Ten machine-learning algorithms were compared. Performance was assessed using AUC, sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), and F1 score. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) supported feature selection and interpretation. An 18-feature random forest model achieved a development-stage cross-validated AUC of 0.93 and external AUCs of 0.89, 0.87, and 0.90. Overall sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, accuracy, and F1 score were 0.78, 0.90, 0.81, 0.91, 0.81, and 0.79, respectively. SHAP identified leukocyte, erythrocyte, and platelet indices as the most important features. A Streamlit application was developed for clinical evaluation. Using a development-derived APL alert threshold of 0.0966, APL sensitivity was 99.02% in development and 96.32%-97.94% across external cohorts, with PPVs of 54.34% and 35.58%-84.25%, respectively. External validation showed center-specific calibration shifts, indicating that predicted probabilities should not be interpreted as universally calibrated absolute diagnostic probabilities. Among patients already confirmed to have APL/M3, AMoL/M5, or ALL, this explainable model enabled low-cost preliminary differentiation using routine hematological data. It may support subtype prioritization and confirmatory testing but cannot replace standard diagnostics, identify other diagnoses, or screen unselected patients. Prospective multinational and workflow-based validation is required before routine implementation.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1939651.abstract: Uterine sarcomas represent a rare and heterogeneous group of malignancies whose management remains clinically challenging. They account for approximately 3%-5% of all uterine malignancies. Undifferentiated uterine sarcoma (UUS) is a subtype of uterine sarcomas. SMARCA4 is a tumor suppressor gene that is aberrantly altered in approximately 5%-7% of human malignancies. SMARCA4-deficient UUS is a highly aggressive, undifferentiated mesenchymal neoplasm associated with a median overall survival (OS) of 7 months. During tumorigenesis, loss of function of either SMARCA4 or SMARCA2 is frequently observed; however, concurrent loss of both genes has been reported to be synthetically lethal and is therefore considered unexpected. In this case report, a 52-year-old Chinese woman with early-stage UUS and SMARCA4 and SMARCA2 co-deficiency underwent surgical resection followed by adjuvant chemotherapy and achieved a disease-free survival (DFS) of 32 months. This case suggests that patients with UUS harboring SMARCA4 and SMARCA2 co-deficiency may derive a survival benefit from early diagnosis and surgical resection. However, owing to the extreme rarity of UUS with co-deficiency of SMARCA4 and SMARCA2, conducting a high-level phase III randomized controlled trial to validate this observation remains impractical.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1940599.abstract: age and ovarian reserve markers are commonly used in clinical practice to predict ovarian response to controlled stimulation for assisted reproductive techniques in infertile patients. In oncofertility, some reports suggest the predictive performance of these markers may be lower in specific subgroups. We evaluated the performance of a prespecified age + log(AMH) model for predicting metaphase-II (MII) oocyte yield in women undergoing oocyte cryopreservation before gonadotoxic treatment. This retrospective single-center cohort study included consecutive oocyte cryopreservation cycles performed before gonadotoxic treatment between January 2015 and January 2025. MII yield was modelled using negative-binomial regression with age and log-transformed AMH as predictors. Regression coefficients were estimated in the current cohort. Model performance was assessed using calibration measures and patient-level bootstrap internal validation, with all cycles from the same woman kept together during resampling. Analyses were performed overall and by cancer type. Threshold-based underestimation analyses and the incremental value of antral follicle count (AFC) were also explored. A total of 179 oocyte cryopreservation cycles performed in 167 women were included. The model showed good overall calibration using aggregated out-of-bootstrap predictions, with calibration-in-the-large of 0.00 (95% CI -0.08 to 0.09) and calibration slope of 0.98 (95% CI 0.80 to 1.15). Mean prediction error was -0.10 MII (95% CI -0.97 to 0.80), indicating minimal average directional bias. Mean absolute error was 4.12 MII (95% CI 3.53 to 4.76), and root mean squared error was 5.94 MII (95% CI 4.92 to 7.00). Substantial underestimation, defined as observed MII yield exceeding predicted yield by more than 4 MII, was more frequent in hematologic malignancies than in solid tumors (31.8% [14/44] vs 12.6% [17/135]; risk difference +19.2 percentage points, 95% CI + 4.4 to +34.1; Fisher's exact p=0.006). This finding remained consistent in the one-cycle-per-woman sensitivity analysis. Adding AFC did not improve predictive performance in the complete-case analysis. age and AMH are useful tools for counseling regarding the expected mature oocyte yield, including in our subset of oncofertility patients. As we found substantial underestimation of mature oocyte yield to be more frequent in hematologic malignancies, the results should be interpreted cautiously in this subgroup.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1941099.abstract: Lipoblastoma-like tumor (LLT) is a distinctive adipocytic neoplasm most commonly arising in the vulva of women. Lingual involvement is extremely rare. Herein, we present a case of LLT occurring in the tongue and review the relevant literature. The patient was a 41-year-old female who presented with a mass on the right lateral border of the tongue for 6 months. Microscopic examination revealed the typical features of LLT. Immunohistochemically, the tumor was positive for CD34 and vimentin, with partial positivity for CDK4 and S-100, and negative for Rb, p16, and MDM2. Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) demonstrated no DDIT3 rearrangement or MDM2 amplification. Next-generation sequencing (NGS) detected no significant genetic alterations. The tumor was completely resected, and no recurrence was observed at 19 months of follow-up. Given the rarity of lingual LLT-of which only three cases, including ours, have been reported-this report expands the current knowledge base and emphasizes the need for accurate diagnosis and long-term patient surveillance.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1941311.abstract: Myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPNs) are driven by constitutive cytokine-receptor signaling, yet the metabolic programs associated with driver genotype and inflammatory remodeling remain incompletely defined. Here we integrated a 60-case clinical MPN cohort, the GSE174060 Affymetrix Human Transcriptome Array 2.0 microarray dataset, immune deconvolution, exploratory feature prioritization, the GSE228995 mouse single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) dataset, human-sample validation, and functional perturbation assays to investigate whether cuproptosis-related metabolism is associated with total calreticulin (CALR) abundance and Janus kinase-signal transducer and activator of transcription (JAK-STAT)-related inflammatory signaling. GSE174060 included 36 samples: 6 essential thrombocythemia (ET), 11 polycythemia vera (PV), 9 primary myelofibrosis (PMF), 4 secondary myelofibrosis (SMF), and 6 healthy control (HC) samples. Clinically, CALR-mutated cases were enriched for thrombocytosis and distinctive megakaryocytic abnormalities, while inflammatory and fibrotic features tracked with higher interleukin-6 (IL-6), tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH). Microarray-based transcriptomic analyses identified an MPN-associated cuproptosis-related and immune-response program, and consensus clustering separated samples into exploratory transcriptomic clusters. Within this expression-derived partition, post hoc multi-algorithm feature prioritization recurrently retained FDX1 and CALR among genes associated with the Cluster 1-versus-Cluster 2 transcriptional contrast. Single-cell analyses localized Calr and Fdx1 across hematopoietic and immune populations and highlighted inferred JAK-STAT-associated communication potential. In human MPN samples, FDX1 and total CALR protein and mRNA levels were increased and accompanied by STAT5 phosphorylation and elevated inflammatory mediators. Functionally, FDX1 knockdown reduced total CALR abundance, STAT5 phosphorylation, cytokine release, sensitivity to copper-dependent cytotoxicity, and proliferation, whereas FDX1 overexpression showed the reciprocal pattern and was partly counteracted by ruxolitinib. These findings support an association between FDX1 perturbation, total CALR abundance, STAT5-associated signaling, and inflammatory output in MPN, but do not establish direct regulation of mutant CALR or mutant CALR-MPL signaling.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1942174.abstract: Concurrent chemoradiotherapy (CCRT) combined with pembrolizumab has become the standard treatment for high-risk locally advanced cervical cancer, increasing the need for prompt recognition of immune-related adverse events (irAEs). We report a rare case of severe gastrointestinal irAE complicated by hepatic portal venous gas (HPVG) during pembrolizumab-based CCRT. A 72-year-old woman with FIGO 2018 stage IIIC1r cervical squamous cell carcinoma developed persistent diarrhea and anorexia during treatment, followed by sudden hematemesis after the first brachytherapy session. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy revealed diffuse gastric mucosal necrosis, while contrast-enhanced computed tomography demonstrated HPVG, intramural gastric gas, and diffuse gastrointestinal wall edema without evidence of intestinal ischemia. Gastric biopsy showed marked intraepithelial lymphocytic infiltration predominantly composed of CD8-positive T cells, consistent with pembrolizumab-induced gastrointestinal irAE. High-dose corticosteroid therapy and supportive conservative management resulted in rapid clinical and radiological resolution, avoiding surgical intervention. This case highlights that gastrointestinal irAEs may mimic conventional CCRT-related toxicities, delaying diagnosis. Furthermore, HPVG should not be considered synonymous with intestinal necrosis. Careful integration of clinical, radiological, endoscopic, and pathological findings is essential to distinguish immune-mediated gastrointestinal injury from ischemic disease and to guide appropriate management.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1942370.abstract: With improved survival among people living with HIV (PLWH), non-AIDS-defining cancers have become increasingly prominent. Women living with HIV (WLWH) remain underrepresented in ovarian cancer trials, leaving limited evidence on the tolerability of standard therapies, including chemotherapy, anti-VEGF agents, and PARP inhibitors. These patients also face unique care barriers beyond biological uncertainties. This retrospective review included five WLWH diagnosed with ovarian cancer (June 2022-March 2024). Three received anticancer treatment; one refused chemotherapy and was lost to follow-up; one had biopsy only. We collected data on demographics, HIV history, tumor characteristics, treatment exposure, adverse events (CTCAE v5.0), CD4+/CD8+ counts, and HIV RNA, focusing safety and immune analyses on the three treated patients. Median age was 51 years; four had stage III-IV disease. No treatment-related deaths, persistent HIV rebound, or AIDS-defining events occurred. During first-line paclitaxel/carboplatin, one patient developed grade 3 neutropenia managed with G-CSF, but later developed significant thrombocytopenia on niraparib requiring dose reduction and hospitalization. Among two patients receiving bevacizumab, CD4+ patterns diverged: one showed a transient decline (387 to 259 cells/μL) with concurrent nedaplatin; another maintained stable counts (150 to 200 cells/μL). One patient had transient, self-limited HIV RNA elevation concurrent with disease progression, which resolved spontaneously. This series provides real-world observations that platinum-based and targeted therapies may be delivered to selected WLWH with close monitoring. The heterogeneous CD4+ responses highlight the need for individualized immune surveillance rather than attributing changes to any single agent. Integrated oncologic-HIV care and attention to socioeconomic barriers remain critical for this underrepresented population.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1943135.abstract: Therapy-related myeloid neoplasms (t-MNs), which develop following cytotoxic chemotherapy or radiotherapy, remain one of the most significant clinical challenges in modern hematology due to their aggressive clinical course and poor survival outcomes. The traditional paradigm regarded the development of t-MNs as a consequence of de novo genetic damage induced by anticancer therapies. However, recent data concerning genomics and clonal evolution have fundamentally transformed our understanding of the biological origins of the disease. Current evidence demonstrates that low-level, clinically silent hematopoietic clones are present in the peripheral blood or bone marrow years prior to disease onset in a substantial proportion of t-MN cases. The pathogenesis of t-MNs is therefore being reconceptualized, not merely as the emergence of de novo treatment-induced mutations, but rather as the expansion and progression to malignant transformation of pre-existing silent clones under selective pressure. Clonal hematopoiesis (CH) is a dynamic biological process characterized by the acquisition of a proliferative advantage by specific cell populations, resulting from somatic mutations accumulated by hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) throughout life. A clinically defined subgroup of this process, including CH of indeterminate potential (CHIP) and clonal cytopenia of undetermined significance (CCUS), are defined as the presence of somatic mutations with a variant allele frequency (VAF) of ≥2% in genes associated with myeloid malignancies. Both are recognized as clinically meaningful pre-cancerous states, differentiated primarily by the presence of unexplained cytopenias in CCUS. The presence of CH by itself is insufficient to drive malignant transformation. The observation that only a small fraction of individuals harboring CHIP or CCUS ultimately develop myeloid neoplasia indicates that clonal progression is not solely dictated by the presence of a mutation, but rather by the biological characteristics of the clone, the specific mutation type, clone size, environmental stressors, and the bone marrow microenvironment. The fundamental paradigm has thus shifted from simply asking "which patients have CH?" to determining "which silent clones possess the potential to evolve into aggressive myeloid neoplasms in the future?" The concept of the "power of silent clones" provides a novel biological perspective in t-MN risk stratification, establishing a foundational framework for the future development of personalized surveillance, early intervention, and targeted preventative strategies. Deciphering CH enables precise risk stratification and helps intercept myeloid malignancies before clinical onset.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1943424.abstract: Aberrant promoter DNA methylation represents an early molecular alteration in oral carcinogenesis and has emerged as a potential source of molecular biomarkers for oral cancer. Although RNF152 has been implicated in cancer-related molecular dysregulation, its promoter methylation and expression status have not previously been specifically investigated in oral premalignant lesions (OPML) or oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC). RNF152 promoter methylation and gene expression were evaluated in paired tumor/lesion and matched adjacent normal tissues from 30 patients with OSCC and 30 patients with OPML, together with oral mucosal tissues from 15 healthy controls. Matched saliva and serum samples from the patient cohorts were also analyzed to evaluate RNF152 methylation as a potential liquid biopsy marker. Quantitative methylation-specific PCR (QMSP) and quantitative real-time PCR (QRT-PCR) were performed, and associations with clinicopathological characteristics, diagnostic performance, and the relationship between promoter methylation and gene expression were investigated. RNF152 promoter methylation was detected in 36.7% of OSCC tumors and 70.0% of OPML lesions, whereas no promoter methylation was identified in oral mucosal tissues from healthy controls. Promoter methylation was also detected in matched saliva and serum samples from both patient groups. Reduced RNF152 expression was observed in 33.3% of OSCC and 30.0% of OPML tissues. Methylation-associated RNF152 expression loss was identified in 13.3% of OSCC and 30.0% of OPML patients. Among methylation-positive cases, concomitant RNF152 expression loss was observed in 36.4% of patients with OSCC and 42.9% of patients with OPML. Continuous promoter methylation levels were not significantly correlated with tissue gene expression in either cohort. RNF152 promoter methylation demonstrated good discriminatory performance for distinguishing OPML from healthy controls (AUC = 0.867, p < 0.001), whereas its discriminatory performance for OSCC was statistically significant but more modest (AUC = 0.683, p = 0.047). This study provides the first comprehensive evaluation of RNF152 promoter methylation and gene expression in oral premalignant lesions and oral squamous cell carcinoma. RNF152 promoter methylation showed greater diagnostic potential for OPML than for OSCC, whereas its performance in liquid biopsy specimens was limited. The incomplete concordance between promoter methylation and gene expression suggests that promoter methylation may contribute to RNF152 downregulation in a subset of cases but is not the sole determinant of its expression. These findings support further evaluation of RNF152 as a candidate component of multimarker epigenetic panels rather than as a standalone diagnostic biomarker. Validation in larger, independent cohorts is required to determine its clinical utility.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1944330.abstract: Intrathyroidal thymic carcinoma (ITTC) with neuroendocrine differentiation is rare, and evidence for definitive radiotherapy in nonsurgical patients remains limited. A 70-year-old woman with a 1-year history of a neck mass and hoarseness was diagnosed with ITTC with neuroendocrine differentiation based on histopathological, immunohistochemical, and imaging findings. After declining surgery and systemic chemotherapy, she received definitive radiotherapy: 60 Gy in 30 fractions to the planning target volume, followed by a sequential boost of 6 Gy in 3 fractions to the gross primary tumor and involved lymph nodes, for a cumulative dose of 66 Gy in 33 fractions. No grade ≥3 acute treatment-related toxicities occurred. At approximately 2 months after radiotherapy, the sum of target-lesion diameters decreased from 54 mm to 42 mm, a 22.2% reduction. With no new lesions or unequivocal progression of non-target disease, the overall response was classified as stable disease according to RECIST 1.1. This case documents early radiographic tumor reduction following definitive radiotherapy for ITTC, although longer follow-up is required to assess the durability of disease control and late toxicity.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1944703.abstract: Genetic variation in DPYD can result in reduced fluoropyrimidine (FP) metabolism and increased risk of severe toxicity. This DPYD test implementation pilot aimed to establish a feasible workflow for DPYD ordering sample collection and FP dose modifications at the University of Florida Health Cancer Institute. Following education on the clinical utility of DPYD testing, a consensus was reached with the University of Florida Health gastrointestinal oncology clinic on an implementation workflow. Novel clinical decision support (CDS) tools were developed including pre- and post-test inline warnings in chemotherapy treatment plans, clickable dose modification buttons, and a pharmacist-facing alert upon medication verification. Primary outcomes were feasibility metrics including rates and timing of test ordering and sample collection, genotype turnaround time, and clinician response to CDS tools (e.g., FP dose modifications). DPYD was ordered for 201 patients between July 2024 and March 2026. Most (180/201) orders were placed prior to chemotherapy in FP-naïve individuals, and 85% (153/180) were also collected pretreatment. The average genotype turnaround time was 5.0 ± 2.7 days. Results were available prior to chemotherapy for 80.3% (114/142) of all patients who received a FP-containing regimen and for 93.2% (110/118) of those with DPYD ordered and collected pretreatment. Nine patients had a deleterious DPYD variant; all who newly initiated a FP-containing regimen received a 50% dose reduction. DPYD test implementation with customized CDS tools to support test ordering and FP prescribing in an academic oncology clinic is feasible, with the majority of results returning prior to chemotherapy. Integrating new and unique processes into already established workflows helps achieve timely test ordering and sample collection.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1945549.abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) remains a major global health burden. Chemotherapy is central to the management of advanced or metastatic disease and is also used in perioperative settings, but outcomes vary substantially. The neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) is an inexpensive and readily available marker of systemic inflammation; its prognostic association in chemotherapy-treated CRC warrants focused evaluation. This study adhered to PRISMA guidelines and was registered with PROSPERO. PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library were searched from inception to July 15, 2025. Studies evaluating pretreatment NLR in relation to overall survival (OS) or a secondary progression- or recurrence-related time-to-event outcome, including progression-free survival (PFS), disease-free survival (DFS), or recurrence-free survival (RFS), in chemotherapy-treated CRC patients were eligible. Study screening, data extraction, and quality assessment were independently conducted by two reviewers. Pooled hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated using random-effects models. Subgroup and leave-one-out sensitivity analyses were performed. Thirty-eight studies (41 cohorts; 11,346 patients) were included. Elevated pretreatment NLR was associated with poorer OS (HR = 1.68, 95% CI 1.54-1.84; P < 0.0001) and poorer progression- or recurrence-related survival (HR = 1.61, 95% CI 1.43-1.81; P < 0.0001). The direction of association was generally consistent across exploratory subgroups defined by treatment category, age, geographic region, and NLR cut-off. Leave-one-out analyses did not identify a single study that changed the direction of either pooled association. Between-study heterogeneity and evidence of small-study effects warrant cautious interpretation. Elevated pretreatment NLR was associated with poorer survival outcomes in chemotherapy-treated CRC. NLR may be a readily available prognostic biomarker, but heterogeneous populations, variable outcome definitions and cut-off values, inconsistent covariate adjustment, and possible small-study effects currently limit its use for clinical decision-making. Prospective validation and methodological standardization are required before routine application. https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/, identifier CRD420251136904.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1945631.abstract: Ewing sarcoma tumors are defined by chromosomal translocations fusing EWSR1 to ETS family genes, most commonly FLI1. The resulting EWS::FLI1 fusion oncoprotein drives tumorigenesis while simultaneously generating unique metabolic and molecular dependencies that may be exploited for Ewing sarcoma-specific therapies. Through analysis of the Cancer Dependency Map (DepMap, Broad Institute), we identified that Ewing sarcoma cell lines exhibit selective sensitivity to loss of genes regulating selenium metabolism compared to other cancer lineages. Ewing sarcoma cells are similarly sensitive to knockout of glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4), a selenoprotein that suppresses ferroptosis, a form of regulated, iron-dependent cell death characterized by the lethal accumulation of lipid peroxides. Using pharmacological inhibitors and targeted degraders of GPX4, as well as genetic knockout approaches, we demonstrate that Ewing sarcoma cells are selectively vulnerable to GPX4 loss or inhibition. We further identify ferroptosis suppressor protein 1 (FSP1) as a modulator of ferroptotic sensitivity in Ewing sarcoma, with FSP1 expression level serving as a determinant of the magnitude of ferroptotic response. Together, these findings establish ferroptosis as a targetable vulnerability in Ewing sarcoma, define GPX4 and FSP1 as key regulators of ferroptotic sensitivity in this disease, and provide a mechanistic rationale for therapeutic strategies targeting the ferroptosis defense axis in Ewing sarcoma tumors.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1946212.abstract: Older patients with lung cancer receiving thoracic radiotherapy have heterogeneous outcomes that are not fully captured by conventional clinical descriptors. We evaluated whether artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted three-dimensional (3D) thoracic body-composition analysis of pretreatment radiotherapy simulation computed tomography (CT) could identify candidate body-composition imaging markers associated with overall survival. This exploratory retrospective single-institution study included 88 patients aged 70 years or older who received thoracic radiotherapy for lung cancer between 2019 and 2021. Thoracic skeletal muscle and intermuscular fat were segmented using an AI-assisted workflow followed by expert review and Hounsfield unit-constrained refinement. Twelve knowledge-informed candidate groups were evaluated using conventional Cox regression. After marker selection, the selected marker pair was assessed in continuous form using bootstrap optimism correction, repeated five-fold cross-validation, and Uno's C-index. Penalized and alternative model-family analysis were performed as exploratory sensitivity analysis. During follow-up, 28 deaths occurred. In an 18-case internal technical validation subset, the raw AI contours achieved Dice similarity coefficients of 0.930 for thoracic skeletal muscle and 0.723 for intermuscular fat. For Group 12, intermuscular adiposity index (IAI) and attenuation-weighted thoracic muscle fraction (TMF) were the variables that met the univariable screening criterion; the resulting two-marker model met the discrimination threshold without problematic collinearity. When modeled together, IAI values above the cohort median (hazard ratio [HR], 2.78; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.25-6.18; P = 0.012) and TMF values above the cohort median (HR, 3.77; 95% CI, 1.52-9.32; P = 0.004) were associated with poorer overall survival. In continuous form, the selected marker pair had an optimism-corrected Harrell's C-index of 0.751 (95% CI, 0.661-0.849), a mean repeated cross-validation C-index of 0.753 ± 0.112, and Uno's C-index of 0.737. These performance estimates were conditional on prior marker selection. AI-assisted analysis of routine radiotherapy simulation CT identified IAI and TMF as candidate body-composition imaging markers associated with overall survival in this clinically heterogeneous cohort. The findings are exploratory and require independent evaluation in larger, clinically characterized cohorts before clinical use.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1948199.abstract: Gastric cancer (GC) is a molecularly heterogeneous disease. This study aims to explore whether endocytosis pathway-associated genes and immune checkpoint-related features were linked to GC subtypes and prognosis. Public transcriptomic datasets from TCGA and GEO were analyzed. ssGSEA was applied to predefined endocytosis-related gene sets, and NMF was used to identify molecular subtypes. Survival, tumor microenvironment features, tumor mutation burden, microsatellite instability, and differentially expressed genes were evaluated. A three-gene prognostic model was developed and assessed through retrospective internal and external validation across public cohorts for prognostic association only. Two endocytosis-related subtypes were identified. The Group 1 subtype showed higher pathway activity, more immunosuppressive microenvironmental features, higher expression of selected immune checkpoint-related markers, and poorer survival. The Group 2 subtype showed lower pathway activity and more favorable outcomes. A three-gene signature (NRP1, SERPINE1, and MISP3) stratified patients into higher-risk and lower-risk groups across retrospective cohorts. Higher-risk cases were associated with worse overall survival and enrichment of epithelial-mesenchymal transition- and immune evasion-related pathways. This retrospective cross-cohort validation suggests that the prognostic signal was not restricted to a single dataset, but it does not demonstrate prospective clinical validity, analytical validity, or readiness for clinical implementation. Endocytosis-related molecular patterns may be associated with distinct biological and prognostic features in GC. The identified subtypes and prognostic signature should be interpreted as exploratory, hypothesis-generating findings that warrant further prospective, functional, and assay-level validation.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1948751.abstract: Anemia represents a frequent and clinically burdensome complication in patients with primary lung cancer receiving platinum-based regimens, yet robust risk stratification tools that integrate multidimensional clinical data and undergo external validation remain scarce. This multicenter study sought to develop and externally validate a machine learning-based predictive model for CIA in this population. A total of 3,434 patients with primary lung cancer were retrospectively enrolled from two geographically distinct institutions, with 3,097 assigned to the training/internal validation set (7:3 split) and 337 retained as an independent external validation set. Variables with missing rates exceeding 30% were excluded, and remaining missing data were imputed using multiple imputation by chained equations (MICE). Thirteen candidate predictors were preselected via univariate screening and least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression. Nine machine learning algorithms were developed and comparatively evaluated using area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), calibration plots, and decision curve analysis. Model interpretability was achieved through SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP). The primary outcome was defined as hemoglobin levels < 100 g/L (CTCAE Grade ≥ 2) recorded during the first two cycles of chemotherapy. Among the nine candidate models, LightGBM achieved the highest discriminative performance, with AUCs of 0.871 (95% CI: 0.852-0.891) in the training set, 0.797 (95% CI: 0.763-0.831) in internal validation, and 0.684 (95% CI: 0.626-0.742) in the external validation set derived from Linfen Central Hospital. Calibration and decision curve analyses consistently demonstrated superior agreement and net clinical benefit for LightGBM across all three datasets. SHAP-based interpretation identified lymphocyte count, D-dimer, alanine aminotransferase, total bilirubin, sex, and albumin as the six most influential predictors, with D-dimer, female sex, and outpatient admission positively associated with anemia risk, whereas lymphocyte count, liver function indices, and albumin showed inverse associations. The LightGBM-based model developed herein demonstrates acceptable and moderate predictive performance, satisfactory calibration, and potential clinical utility across geographically diverse populations, offering a preliminary risk-stratification tool for early identification of lung cancer patients at elevated anemia risk prior to chemotherapy initiation. However, given the modest external validation performance, cautious interpretation and further refinement are warranted before widespread clinical deployment.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1948986.abstract: Introduction Patients with advanced solid tumors and severe hepatic dysfunction have limited systemic therapy options due to impaired drug metabolism and increased toxicity risks. This population is often excluded from clinical trials, leaving a critical treatment gap. This study evaluates the feasibility, safety, pharmacokinetics and efficacy of S-1, an oral prodrug of 5-fluorouracil (5-FU), plus cisplatin in these patients. Methods Between September 2016 and November 2023, 61 patients were enrolled into four cohorts based on hepatic function per NCI-ODWG criteria: normal (Cohort 1), mild (Cohort 2), moderate (Cohort 3), and severe dysfunction (Cohort 4). Primary endpoints were safety and 5-fluorouracil pharmacokinetics; secondary endpoints included objective response rate (ORR) and 3-month clinical benefit rate (3M-CBR). Results On Cycle 1 day 15, patients with severe hepatic dysfunction (Cohort 4) had lower 5-FU C max and longer T max than those with normal hepatic function (Cohort 1) (p<0.05), though 5-FU AUC remained comparable across cohorts. Safety in Cohort 4 were similar to those in Cohorts 1–3. No grade 5 treatment-related adverse events occurred. In Cohort 4, 22.2% achieved a partial response, 40.7% derived clinical benefit, and 22.2% maintained progression-free survival ≥6 months, providing preliminary evidence of clinical activity in this population. Conclusion Patients with severe hepatic dysfunction had similar 5-FU AUC and toxicities to those with less severe hepatic dysfunction, and preliminary evidence of clinical activity was observed with cisplatin + S-1. These findings provide prospective preliminary evidence that this combination may be feasible in selected patients with severe hepatic dysfunction, a population frequently excluded from clinical trials. Larger studies are needed to further define its safety, pharmacokinetics, and clinical activity in this population. (Clinical Trial Registration: NCT03519074. Retrospectively registered 08 May 2018).

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1950737.abstract: Cancer treatment-related oral mucositis (OM) is one of the most common adverse effects of cancer treatment and can substantially impair patients' quality of life. Its effective management depends heavily on patients' continuous self-management. This scoping review aimed to systematically map the intervention components, delivery modes, and existing limitations of self-management support interventions, thereby providing evidence to inform the optimization of intervention strategies. A scoping review was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews. Seven databases, including PubMed, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, CINAHL, Embase, China National Knowledge Infrastructure, and WanFang, were searched from inception to May 10, 2026. Two reviewers independently screened titles, abstracts, and full texts according to predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. Data were charted using a standardized form and summarized using descriptive numerical and content analyses. A total of 7,132 records were identified, and 16 studies were ultimately included, comprising 9 quasi-experimental studies, 6 randomized controlled trials, and 1 mixed-methods study. The interventions were primarily hospital-based and nurse-led, with some incorporating digital tools or written materials. Reported outcomes generally included OM-related clinical outcomes, quality of life, self-management-related outcomes, and nutritional status, although the direction and magnitude of findings varied across studies. Existing studies have reported potential improvements in OM-related and self-management-related outcomes following self-management support interventions. However, these findings should be interpreted cautiously because of heterogeneity in study designs, intervention components, and outcome measures, together with the absence of critical appraisal. Further well-designed studies using standardized outcome measures are needed to strengthen the evidence base.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1953570.abstract: Autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (ASCT) is the standard consolidation therapy for multiple myeloma (MM), but its widespread implementation is constrained by the high cost and limited availability of conventional laminar airflow rooms. The air-flow bed, a single-bed unit equipped with high-efficiency particulate air (HEPA) filtration providing class 100 (ISO class 5) air quality, represents a more accessible and cost-effective alternative. In this retrospective cohort study, we compared the efficacy, safety, and costs of ASCT performed in air-flow beds (Group A, n=91) versus conventional laminar airflow rooms (Group B, n=60) in 151 MM patients treated between 2022 and 2026. Multivariable regression models were adjusted for potential confounders. Sepsis was analyzed descriptively because of the small number of events. Platelet transfusion requirements were analyzed using negative binomial regression. Engraftment outcomes were comparable between groups. Group A showed significantly lower rates of mucositis, diarrhea, and nausea/vomiting, and no sepsis events occurred in Group A compared with four cases (6.7%) in Group B. Pathogen detection rate was lower in Group A than in Group B (5.5% vs. 15.0%, P = 0.050). In negative binomial regression, air-flow bed use was independently associated with a lower number of platelet transfusion units (IRR = 0.50, P<0.001). Higher CD34+ cell dose was also independently associated with fewer platelet transfusions (IRR = 0.94 per 1×106/kg increase, P = 0.003). Sepsis occurred exclusively in Group B (4/60, 6.7% vs. 0/91, 0%). With only four events and complete separation between groups, multivariable logistic regression was not statistically reliable. This finding is therefore reported descriptively and no adjusted effect estimate is presented. Median total costs were significantly lower in Group A (¥121,738 [approximately $16,908] vs. ¥137,506 [approximately $19,098], P = 0.0002). No transplant-related mortality occurred in Group A, whereas one patient (1.7%) in Group B died. These findings suggest that air-flow beds may represent a safe, effective, and economically viable alternative to conventional laminar airflow rooms for ASCT in MM. Because protective environment and transplant era were strongly intertwined, these observational associations should be interpreted with caution and regarded as hypothesis-generating. Prospective validation in randomized controlled trials is warranted to confirm these observations.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1954382.abstract: Oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) is the most common malignant tumor in the head and neck region. In locally advanced patients, neoadjuvant chemotherapy centered on cisplatin and 5-fluorouracil often leads to primary/acquired resistance, with a 5-year survival rate of less than 50%. Tumor microenvironment (TME) immunosuppressive remodeling is the core cause of chemotherapy failure. Adipokines secreted by cancer-associated adipocytes (CAAs) are the key mediators that link metabolic disorders, immune polarization and chemotherapy resistance. The adipokines leptin, adiponectin, chemerin, resistin, and GDF15 signal through pathways such as JAK2/STAT3, PI3K/AKT, NF-κB, and PPARγ to bidirectionally regulate the polarization phenotypes of tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs), myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), CD4+/CD8+ T cells, and NK cells. Pro-cancer adipokines induce M2-type TAMs, MDSCs expansion, Th2/Th17 polarization, and effector T cell exhaustion, constructing an immunosuppressive microenvironment, upregulating DNA damage repair, drug efflux, and anti-apoptotic genes, and reducing cisplatin/5-FU chemosensitivity. The tumor-suppressive adipokine adiponectin promotes M1 macrophage and CD8+ effector T cell infiltration, reverses immunosuppression, and sensitizes chemotherapy. This article systematically reviews the origin and classification of adipokines, the polarization patterns of immune cells in the OSCC microenvironment, the molecular pathways by which various adipokines regulate immune polarization, and the complete mechanism by which immune polarization mediates chemotherapy resistance. It summarizes the value of clinical markers and targeted reversal strategies, points out current research bottlenecks, and looks forward to the translational prospects of metabolism-immunotherapy combined with chemotherapy, aiming to provide new metabolism-immune targets for overcoming chemotherapy resistance in oral cancer.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1954599.abstract: Mismatch repair deficiency defines an immunologically distinct subgroup of endometrioid endometrial carcinoma, but its relationship with CD163-positive macrophage infiltration in early-stage disease remains incompletely characterized. We evaluated the association between MMR status and quantitative CD163-positive TAM infiltration, together with secondary clinicopathologic and exploratory DFS analyses. This single-center retrospective cohort included patients with surgically treated FIGO 2009 stage I-II endometrioid endometrial carcinoma and available formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tumor tissue. Immunohistochemistry for MLH1, PMS2, MSH2, MSH6, and CD163 defined MMR status and quantified macrophage density. CD163-positive TAM density was analyzed quantitatively as the principal measure, with a cohort-median low/high categorization retained for secondary phenotypic analyses. Median regression evaluated the association between MMR status and continuous CD163-positive TAM density, whereas logistic regression was used for the secondary binary TAM analysis and the composite adverse pathologic endpoint. Exploratory DFS analyses included single-marker and combined Cox models, formal MMR-by-TAM interaction testing, and comparison of models with and without continuous CD163-positive TAM density. Among 254 patients assessed, 236 were included. MMR protein expression was retained in 172 tumors (72.9%), whereas 64 (27.1%) were classified as dMMR. CD163-positive TAM density was higher in dMMR than pMMR tumors (median, 76 vs 47 cells/HPF; P<0.001), and high TAM infiltration was more frequent in dMMR tumors (44/64, 68.8% vs 71/172, 41.3%; P<0.001). After adjustment for age, FIGO stage, tumor grade, tumor size, and deep myometrial invasion, dMMR remained associated with high macrophage infiltration (adjusted OR, 2.27; 95% CI, 1.19-4.18; P = 0.008). High macrophage infiltration was associated with grade 3 histology, deep myometrial invasion, LVSI, and the composite adverse pathologic feature; the association with the composite endpoint persisted after adjustment (adjusted OR, 1.78; 95% CI, 1.01-3.14; P = 0.047). During follow-up, 26 DFS events occurred. In exploratory Cox analyses, dMMR was associated with DFS (adjusted HR, 2.76; 95% CI, 1.25-6.10; P = 0.012), whereas continuous CD163-positive TAM density was not (adjusted HR per 10 cells/HPF, 1.04; 95% CI, 0.97-1.12; P = 0.281), and addition of CD163-positive TAM density did not significantly improve model fit beyond MMR status (likelihood-ratio P = 0.279). The dMMR/high-TAM phenotype retained an exploratory association with DFS in the conventional model (adjusted HR, 2.21; 95% CI, 1.02-4.81; P = 0.044), but the association was attenuated after additional adjustment for adjuvant therapy (HR, 2.04; 95% CI, 0.93-4.52; P = 0.075). IHC-defined dMMR was associated with increased CD163-positive macrophage infiltration, and higher TAM infiltration was associated with adverse pathologic features. DFS findings were exploratory and did not establish incremental prognostic value of CD163-positive TAM infiltration beyond MMR status; larger externally validated cohorts are required to assess prognostic relevance.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1955408.abstract: Mushroom-derived polysaccharides are widely promoted as anticancer immune modulators, but interpretation is weakened by imprecise product identity, chemically non-equivalent preparations, and extrapolation across evidence levels. This critical narrative review evaluates beta-glucans, heteropolysaccharides, polysaccharide-protein complexes, crude fractions, modified derivatives, and multicomponent extracts as preparation-specific adjunct candidates. Receptor-level evidence is strongest for general fungal beta-glucan systems, particularly Dectin-1/Syk/CARD9 signaling and conditional complement receptor 3 cooperation; direct transfer of those mechanisms to individual mushroom preparations requires product-specific causal testing. Selected animal studies support myeloid remodeling, dendritic-cell and natural-killer-cell effects, and T-cell activation, but route, exposure, product characterization, and model limitations constrain translation. Human evidence remains heterogeneous: historical randomized PSK studies reported benefit in specific adjuvant chemotherapy settings, a later phase III lentinan trial was negative for overall survival, and small maitake, Agaricus, and pleuran studies mainly report immune surrogates. Direct clinical evidence with checkpoint inhibitors, therapeutic antibodies, or cancer vaccines is not established. The field should therefore move from species-level claims to product-level development with authenticated source material, orthogonal structural analysis, contaminant control, mechanism-linked potency, route-specific pharmacokinetics, tumor pharmacodynamics, and randomized testing against contemporary standard care. Mushroom-derived polysaccharide immunomodulators remain plausible research candidates, but neither the class nor unstandardized mushroom foods or supplements are clinically validated substitutes for established cancer treatment.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1956522.abstract: Multiple myeloma (MM) outcomes have improved with proteasome inhibitors, immunomodulatory drugs, anti-CD38 antibodies, and transplantation, yet a subset of patients with high-risk MM (HRMM) continues to relapse early and die prematurely. Immune effector therapies (IET)-B-cell maturation antigen (BCMA)- and G protein-coupled receptor class C group 5 member D (GPRC5D)-directed chimeric antigen receptor T cells (CAR-T) and bispecific antibodies-have transformed the treatment of relapsed/refractory MM. However, their benefit in HRMM remains incompletely defined. This review describes how HRMM is defined in the IET-era distinguishing baseline biological/genomic risk, clinical high-risk phenotypes, and IET-specific adverse predictors. The International Myeloma Society/International Myeloma Working Group consensus integrates adverse cytogenetics and beta-2 microglobulin, whereas functional high-risk disease, extramedullary disease (EMD), plasma cell leukemia (PCL), high tumor burden, inflammation, and prior BCMA exposure identify aggressive disease in relapsed patients. Across pivotal trials, CAR-T therapy, particularly ciltacabtagene autoleucel, and selected bispecific antibodies retain activity in high-risk cytogenetic subgroups, whereas EMD and PCL remain associated with inferior responses and short progression-free survival. Emerging dual-antigen and trispecific engagers, along with novel targets such as FcRH5 and CD70, aim to overcome antigen escape. Prospective, biology-informed studies are needed to achieve durable disease control in HRMM.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1957030.abstract: Cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT)-based adaptive radiotherapy (ART) has emerged as a promising strategy for addressing inter-fractional anatomical and physiological changes during treatment. By incorporating on-treatment imaging, ART enables treatment plans to be adapted to the anatomy of the day, with the potential to improve target coverage and reduce dose exposure to organs at risk (OARs). However, routine implementation remains constrained by the limited image quality of CBCT, uncertainties in dose calculation, labour-intensive workflows and the lack of reliable criteria for determining when adaptation is clinically necessary. This review summarises the development, current status and future prospects of CBCT-based ART, with particular emphasis on artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted automated delineation and automated radiotherapy decision-making systems. CBCT is widely available on modern linear accelerators and remains the most practical imaging basis for ART in many centres. Nevertheless, poor soft-tissue contrast, noise, artefacts, field-of-view truncation and unstable Hounsfield unit values limit its performance in target delineation and dose reconstruction. Recent advances in image-quality enhancement, deformable image registration and synthetic CT generation have partially addressed these limitations. AI-based auto-segmentation models, including convolutional neural networks, Transformers, generative adversarial networks and diffusion models, have demonstrated increasingly favourable geometric accuracy and workflow efficiency. Automated decision-making systems can advise clinicians whether treatment-plan adaptation is required and how it should be implemented according to each patient's circumstances, representing a prerequisite for more efficient ART. Current research has mainly focused on two approaches: adaptation triggered by predefined dosimetric thresholds, and artificial-intelligence-based models that learn from prior knowledge and predict potential dosimetric changes for the current patient based on previous experience. Both approaches have their respective strengths and limitations, but require further refinement, including the systematic exploration of decision thresholds. Moreover, the realisation of fully automated adaptive radiotherapy will require the integration of additional systems, including automated treatment planning and automated QA. Overall, CBCT-based ART assisted by AI is technically feasible and may improve dosimetric quality and treatment efficiency. Future progress requires improved CBCT-specific algorithms, integrated automated planning and QA, multicentre validation, standardised safety frameworks and stronger evidence of clinical benefit.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1957407.abstract: To evaluate 5.0-T ultra-high-field multi-parametric diffusion MRI (mp-dMRI) combined with histogram analysis for assessing the pathological grade, stage, and adverse pathological factors in prostate cancer (PCa). This retrospective study included 138 patients with histopathologically confirmed PCa. All patients underwent preoperative 5.0-T MRI, including diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI), diffusion kurtosis imaging (DKI), and intravoxel incoherent motion (IVIM) sequences. Histogram parameters were extracted from parametric maps of the apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC), mean diffusivity (MD), mean kurtosis (MK), true diffusion coefficient (D), perfusion fraction (f), etc. using 3D Slicer software. Between-group comparisons were performed using the Mann-Whitney U test or the independent-samples t-test, as appropriate. Spearman's rank correlation analysis was used to evaluate the relationships between histogram parameters and both the ISUP grade group (ISUP GG) and pathological T stage (pT). Logistic regression was used for variable selection and model construction. Diagnostic performance was assessed using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis. Among the 138 patients, most histogram parameters of ADC, MD, MK, D, and f differed significantly between clinically significant PCa (csPCa) and clinically insignificant PCa (ciPCa). For distinguishing csPCa from ciPCa, D_90th percentile achieved the highest AUC among single parameters (0.756). Univariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses identified ADC_mean, MD_Minimum, D_90th percentile, and f_Maximum as independent predictors across the DWI, DKI, and IVIM sequences. The combined model comprising these four parameters achieved an AUC of 0.809. After internal validation using bootstrap resampling (1,000 repetitions), the resulting AUC was 0.808, indicating good model robustness. Further correlation analysis showed that multiple histogram parameters of ADC, MD, MK, D, and f also demonstrated mild to moderate correlations with ISUP GG and pT stage. D_RMS and MD_skewness exhibited the strongest correlations with ISUP GG and pT stage, respectively (r = -0.458 and r = 0.443, both P < 0.001). Finally, among the 60 surgical patients, multiple histogram features of ADC, MD, MK, D, and f differed significantly between patients with and without EPE, SVI, PSM, and PNI. Quantitative histogram parameters derived from 5.0-T ultra-high-field mp-dMRI show promise for the non-invasive assessment of tumor aggressiveness and adverse prognostic factors in PCa.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1957728.abstract: Background KRAS-mutated ultra-low rectal cancer is associated with poor response to conventional neoadjuvant therapy, making sphincter preservation particularly challenging. In addition, effective rehabilitation strategies for severe low anterior resection syndrome (LARS) remain limited. Case presentation A 55-year-old woman with KRAS-mutated ultra-low rectal adenocarcinoma experienced insufficient tumor regression after multiple lines of chemotherapy, chemoradiotherapy, and immunotherapy, complicated by oxaliplatin allergy. After referral to our center, she received bevacizumab plus XELIRI combined with traditional Chinese medicine therapies. Following five treatment cycles, the patient underwent laparoscopic radical rectal resection with transanal specimen extraction and Bacon-type pull-through reconstruction. Pathological examination demonstrated negative proximal, distal, and circumferential margins, no metastatic involvement among 12 examined lymph nodes, and a final pathological stage of ypT2N0. The patient subsequently developed major LARS and underwent a four-week rehabilitation program centered on electroacupuncture at the Baliao acupoints. Assessment was conducted using the LARS score, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center Bowel Function Instrument (MSKCC-BFI), and EORTC QLQ-C30 scales. The patient’s bowel movement frequency decreased from over 30 times per day to approximately 10 times, and remained stable at 7–10 times during the 6-month follow-up. Conclusion In this patient, an individualized conversion strategy was followed by R0 sphincter-preserving resection, and postoperative bowel function improved temporally during and after multimodal rehabilitation that included electroacupuncture. This observation provide preliminary evidence in support of this treatment approach. However, high-quality studies are still required to comprehensively evaluate the efficacy of this treatment regimen.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1959029.abstract: Pancreatic hamartoma (PH) is an exceedingly rare benign non-neoplastic lesion of the pancreas. Owing to its nonspecific clinical and radiological features, it is prone to misdiagnosis. Among its various subtypes, functionally active pancreatic hamartomas with distinct endocrine activity have only been sporadically reported in the literature as individual cases. We report the case of a 58-year-old female patient whose initial presentation was characterized by paroxysmal behavioral abnormalities during nocturnal sleep, manifesting as sudden agitation, arm-flinging, and purposeless stereotyped movements after sleep onset. During these episodes, the patient exhibited a confusional state with subsequent complete amnesia for the events, a clinical phenotype highly suggestive of REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD) or frontal lobe epilepsy. In-hospital monitoring revealed refractory nocturnal hypoglycemia. Imaging studies identified a mass in the pancreatic tail, and the patient underwent laparoscopic distal pancreatectomy. Postoperative histopathological and immunohistochemical examination confirmed the diagnosis of pancreatic hamartoma, composed predominantly of islet cells (approximately 90%) with associated islet cell tumor-like hyperplasia. Following surgery, the patient's nocturnal hypoglycemia and sleep-related behavioral abnormalities resolved completely.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1959240.abstract: The process of chronic gastritis transforming into gastric cancer (GC) follows the classic Correa cascade, with persistent inflammation driving the stepwise transition from normal gastric mucosa through superficial gastritis, atrophic gastritis, intestinal metaplasia, dysplasia, and ultimately carcinoma. Among these stages, intestinal metaplasia and dysplasia occurring on an atrophic mucosal background are widely regarded as the most common gastric precancerous lesions (GPL) because of their pronounced carcinogenic risk. Chronic inflammation can induce epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), thereby accelerating gastric malignant progression. In the GPL stage, the inflammatory gastric microenvironment commonly induces partial EMT (pEMT); importantly, this state is partly reversible and may be amenable to intervention to slow disease progression. As lesions advance, epithelial cells more fully undergo EMT, acquiring greater motility, invasiveness, and metastatic capability, which increases susceptibility to malignant conversion. MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are key molecular regulators in the transition from chronic gastritis to GC through EMT modulation. This review comprehensively discusses inflammation-driven EMT activation and functionally classifies pro-EMT oncomiRNAs (e.g., miR-21, miR-155) and anti-EMT tumor-suppressive miRNAs (e.g., miR-200 family, let-7 family, miR-34a), delineating a complex crosstalk network among inflammation, miRNA, and EMT. We further evaluate miRNAs as non-invasive biomarkers for early detection and prognosis of GPL and discuss emerging therapeutic strategies targeting the miRNA-EMT axis, including nanoparticle- or exosome-based delivery systems, miRNA antagonists, and miRNA sponges. Nevertheless, clinical application of circulating miRNAs remains limited by insufficient assay standardization and validation, incomplete target specificity, off-target effects, suboptimal delivery efficiency, and a lack of large-scale clinical evidence. By integrating molecular mechanisms and transformation status of miRNA-EMT axis in GPL, this review provides new insights for precision prevention and targeted intervention in gastric carcinogenesis.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1959750.abstract: Background Nigeria bears one of the world’s largest burdens of HIV, with ongoing expansion of antiretroviral therapy (ART) significantly improving the survival of people living with HIV (PLHIV). This epidemiologic shift has changed the pattern of morbidity and mortality toward chronic conditions, especially HIV-associated malignancies (HIVAMs), including both AIDS-defining malignancies (ADMs) and non-AIDS-defining malignancies (NADMs). Despite their increasing significance, the national burden, patterns, and systemic challenges related to HIVAMs in Nigeria remain poorly understood and characterized. Methods We conducted a narrative review of peer-reviewed literature, cancer registry reports, and grey literature published between January 2000 and December 2024. Searches were carried out in PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, African Journals Online, and Google Scholar, complemented by national reports from the National Agency for the Control of AIDS, the Federal Ministry of Health, and the National System of Cancer Registries. Eligible sources reported cancer occurrence among PLHIV or HIV prevalence among cancer patients in Nigeria. Findings were synthesized narratively due to significant heterogeneity across study designs and outcomes. Results Seventy-three sources met the inclusion criteria, and these were primarily hospital-based and retrospective studies. ADMs remain the most common cancers among PLHIV, notably invasive cervical cancer, Kaposi sarcoma, and non-Hodgkin lymphoma, with notable regional differences. Expansion of ART has been linked to a decline in Kaposi sarcoma incidence, while the burden of cervical cancer remains high, driven by persistent oncogenic HPV infection and limited screening coverage among women living with HIV (WLWH). Emerging NADMs, such as hepatocellular carcinoma, Hodgkin lymphoma, breast cancer, and ocular surface squamous neoplasia, reflect improved survival, aging, chronic immune dysregulation, and co-infections like Hepatitis B and C. Across these cancers, late-stage presentation and poor outcomes are common, largely due to fragmented HIV–cancer surveillance, inadequate pathology and radiotherapy capacity, limited molecular diagnostics, high out-of-pocket treatment costs, and weak integration of HIV and oncology services. Conclusion HIV-associated cancers pose a major yet often overlooked public health issue in Nigeria. Enhancing integrated HIV–cancer surveillance, increasing prevention and early detection efforts through ART programs, upgrading diagnostic and treatment facilities, and utilizing digital and molecular innovations are essential for decreasing preventable cancer-related morbidity and mortality among PLHIV in Nigeria.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1960553.abstract: Tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) are abundant and functionally diverse components of the lung tumor microenvironment (TME) and are associated with therapeutic response and resistance in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Durable responses to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) and targeted therapies remain limited, with TAM-associated immune evasion and therapy-refractory microenvironments representing potentially relevant components of this resistance landscape. This narrative review prioritizes evidence from human NSCLC specimens and clinically annotated cohorts, especially from single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) and spatial transcriptomics, while integrating relevant mechanistic evidence from NSCLC experimental systems, animal models, and related cancer contexts. Moving beyond the M1/M2 paradigm, we synthesize convergent findings to describe recurring, niche-resolved TAM programs. Across NSCLC, we highlight recurrent SPP1-associated, TREM2-associated, and C1q/LAM-like macrophage programs as a practical framework for integrating recurrent TAM states across spatial and treatment contexts. We propose an integrative framework in which TAM state dynamics are associated with, and may contribute to, therapy-refractory phenotypes during (i) ICI therapy through immune exclusion, (ii) oncogene-targeted therapy through macrophage-associated bypass signaling and survival plasticity, particularly in EGFR-TKI resistance, and (iii) post-radiochemotherapy microenvironmental remodeling, with potential implications for residual disease ecosystems that require further clinical validation, particularly with respect to recurrence and relapse. TAM program signatures and spatial organization provide a rationale for investigating biomarker-guided stratification and macrophage-directed combination strategies targeting state-niche axes. Future work should prioritize clinically validated, state- and niche-resolved multimodal biomarkers and prospective translational studies to support rational pairing with ICIs and targeted therapies.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1962784.abstract: Ginsenoside Rb2 has demonstrated antitumor activity in multiple malignancies, yet its role in cervical cancer and the underlying mechanism remain unclear. This study investigated the effects of Rb2 on cervical cancer progression and explored whether metabolic reprogramming contributes to PD-L1 regulation. Cell proliferation, migration, invasion, glycolytic activity, lactate production, histone lactylation, and PD-L1 expression were evaluated in cervical cancer cells using CCK-8, EdU, colony formation, wound-healing, Transwell, Seahorse analysis, RT-qPCR, western blotting, flow cytometry, and ChIP-qPCR. LDHA regulation was examined by protein and mRNA stability assays, pharmacological inhibition, lysosome immunoprecipitation, gain- and loss-of-function studies, co-immunoprecipitation, molecular docking, and biotinylated Rb2 pull-down assays. T-cell function was assessed by Jurkat T-cell-tumor cell co-culture and IL-2 ELISA. Xenograft models and clinical samples were used for validation. Rb2 significantly inhibited cervical cancer cell proliferation, migration, invasion, and xenograft tumor growth, reducing HeLa and SiHa cell viability by approximately 23.4% and 25.7%, respectively. Rb2 selectively downregulated PD-L1 and suppressed glycolysis and lactate production, with reduced H3K18la/H4K12la lactylation at the PD-L1 promoter. LDHA was the primary glycolytic enzyme reduced by Rb2, without changes in its mRNA. Rb2 decreased LDHA protein stability and promoted its autophagy-lysosome-dependent degradation, with p62 required and the p62-LDHA interaction enhanced by Rb2. Rb2-pretreated tumor cells restored IL-2 production by co-cultured Jurkat T cells, whereas LDHA overexpression reversed this effect. LDHA overexpression partially rescued Rb2's effects, and LDHA correlated positively with PD-L1 in cervical cancer tissues. Rb2 suppresses cervical cancer progression by promoting p62-dependent autophagic degradation of LDHA, thereby inhibiting glycolysis-associated H3K18la and PD-L1 transcription. These findings reveal a p62/LDHA/H3K18la/PD-L1 signaling axis through which Rb2 exerts its antitumor effects.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1963032.abstract: To determine whether heterogeneous genomic alterations detected by clinical tumor panels converge on a reproducible pathway-level difference between hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and cholangiocarcinoma (CCA), and to examine its transcriptional output, cellular localization, and tumor-stromal coexpression context in public multi-omics cohorts. The institutional cohort comprised 52 patients who underwent tumor tissue genomic testing, including 28 with HCC and 24 in a CCA working cohort whose intrahepatic location was not uniformly documented. Ten canonical oncogenic pathways were compared using panel-aware evaluable denominators, and the selected pathway was tested in independent Memorial Sloan Kettering (MSK) cohorts. Matched genomic and transcriptomic data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) were used to evaluate downstream pathway activity. GSE151530 and GSE189903 were analyzed by patient-level pseudobulk to localize the transcriptional difference, followed by CellChatDB-guided ligand-receptor coexpression analysis. Receptor tyrosine kinase-RAS (RTK-RAS) showed the strongest cancer-type difference in the institutional cohort: alterations were detected in 4/21 evaluable HCC cases and 8/11 evaluable CCA cases (odds ratio [OR] = 9.44; 95% CI, 1.87-47.70; P = 0.00601; Benjamini-Hochberg-adjusted q = 0.0601), with concordant directions across sensitivity analyses. In MSK, integrated RTK-RAS alterations occurred in 240/412 intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (iCCA) cases (58.3%) and 107/289 HCC cases (37.0%; OR = 2.37; 95% CI, 1.74-3.22; P = 3.12 × 10-8). In TCGA, RTK-RAS status was associated with higher mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) activity in the pooled cancer-type-adjusted model (β = 0.240; 95% CI, 0.051-0.428; P = 0.0129), whereas the within-iCCA estimate was positive but imprecise. Patient-level single-cell meta-analysis localized the higher iCCA MAPK activity predominantly to malignant cells (pooled effect = 1.455; 95% CI, 0.658-2.252; P = 3.46 × 10-4; q = 0.00208). Platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF)-PDGFRA and insulin-like growth factor (IGF)-IGF1R coexpression patterns accompanied this malignant-cell phenotype. Panel-aware integration of clinical genomic testing and public multi-omics data supports a higher burden of heterogeneous RTK-RAS alterations in CCA/iCCA than in HCC and links this difference to a malignant-cell MAPK transcriptional phenotype. The pathway-level framework complements, rather than replaces, established alteration-specific interpretation and generates tumor-stromal coexpression hypotheses for further spatial and functional testing.
